From it the authors derive 14 indicator properties: RPT-1–2, GWT-1–4, HOT-1–4, AST-1, PP-1 and AE-1–2. The claim for them is only that more of them raises the probability of consciousness. They assess a handful of systems against subsets of the list and conclude that no current system "appears to be a strong candidate". Transformer LLMs have "only a relatively weak case" for any GWT indicator, because a single forward pass has no recurrence or global broadcast. Perceiver arguably has GWT-1, GWT-2 and half of GWT-4 but lacks broadcast. Among the embodied agents, AdA is the likeliest to meet AE-2. Most indicators could be built with standard ML techniques. | [LIT-085](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-085.md) v3 | The No-U-Turn Sampler: Adaptively Setting Path Lengths in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo | Hoffman & Gelman (2011), [ARXIV-1111.4246](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.4246). NUTS removes HMC's step-count L. It doubles a leapfrog trajectory forwards and backwards in random directions until some balanced subtree satisfies (θ⁺−θ⁻)·r⁻ < 0 or (θ⁺−θ⁻)·r⁺ < 0. It keeps detailed balance by slice sampling and by excluding states that could not have regenerated the tree. With ε set by a dual-averaging scheme (γ = 0.05, t₀ = 10, κ = 0.75, target δ ≈ 0.6), it matched the best hand-tuned HMC in ESS per gradient on two logistic-regression posteriors. It beat that HMC by about 3× on a 250-D Gaussian and on a 3001-D stochastic-volatility model (§4.4). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-081); This is the source of the default sampler in Stan, PyMC and NumPyro, and it is worth reading for its derivation. The algorithm as run today, with multinomial rather than slice selection and adapted mass matrices, is documented elsewhere. A reader who wants current practice should read this paper together with that later account. |

| [LIT-226](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-226.md) v2 | The Conditional Entropy Bottleneck | Fischer (2020), [ARXIV-2002.05379](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05379). The Conditional Entropy Bottleneck minimizes I(X;Z\|Y) − γI(Y;Z), which is the Information Bottleneck with γ = β − 1, aimed at the "Minimum Necessary Information" point I(X;Y) = I(X;Z) = I(Y;Z). On Fashion MNIST it improves accuracy, adversarial robustness, OoD detection and calibration over VIB and deterministic baselines, and it does not memorize random labels. The chaos half largely re-measures Frankle et al.'s (2020) spawning / linear-mode-connectivity result with a parameter perturbation in place of fresh SGD noise, and the claimed role of the cone in generalisation is asserted. What would settle it: seeds and error bars, the batch size, a stated perturbation norm, other domains, and a quantitative test of confinement (e.g. an angular radius that stops growing) rather than a 3-D picture. |
| [LIT-386](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-386.md) v2 | Homeostasis and soft robotics in the design of feeling machines | Man & Damasio (2019), Nature Machine Intelligence 1:446–452. A perspective proposing machines organized around homeostasis: a body that must be kept within viable states gives the machine a goal of its own, and something like feeling as a source of motivation and of evaluation. Soft robotics and multisensory abstraction are named as the means. The claimed payoffs are equivalents of feeling, better function across environments, and a platform for studying consciousness. Unread: placed from the abstract. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-01 at the owner's request; no full text could be reached, so it is placed from the abstract and figure captions only and no NOTE is filed. Nature's page is paywalled, there is no arXiv version, Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar list no open copy, and the ResearchGate, Scribd and ProQuest copies did not serve the text. By its abstract it is a design proposal for machines built around homeostasis, not a reported system or result. Flagged anthology-candidate because the anthology's agents-and-environments topic could hold it; a reading should settle whether it carries an instruction for ML practice. |
| [LIT-427](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-427.md) | Pandemonium: A Paradigm for Learning | Selfridge (1959), Mechanisation of Thought Processes Vol. I (HMSO), pp. 513–526 plus discussion to p. 531. Pattern recognition by a "pandemonium": data demons hold the input, computational subdemons compute features, each cognitive demon "shrieks" a weighted sum of them, and a decision demon picks the loudest. The system learns by hill-climbing on the weights and by "natural selection" on the subdemons, culling those of low worth and breeding new ones by mutation and by "conjugation" of pairs. It is applied to telling dots from dashes in hand-keyed Morse. In the discussion McCarthy proposes reading the demons' private computation as unconscious and their public shouting as conscious thought. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-360](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-360.md)); worth reading as the first published architecture of a mind-like process built from many quasi-independent "demons", each doing one narrow job, with no part holding the whole's competence. That is the decomposition template that Minsky's agents inherit. Cite it as an engineering proposal with a preliminary result reported only in discussion, not as a theory of mind. Its one remark on consciousness is McCarthy's, in the discussion, and it is an aside. |
| [LIT-436](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-436.md) | Intelligence without representation | Brooks (1991), Artificial Intelligence 47:139–159, written in 1987. Argues that AI should be built incrementally from complete autonomous "Creatures" tested in the real world, and that the system should be decomposed by activity into parallel layers, each connecting sensing to action, not by function into perception, a central reasoner and action. His robots have no central representation and no central control: each layer is a fixed network of simple finite-state machines, and a higher layer subsumes a lower one by suppressing or inhibiting its wires. Coherent behaviour emerges, "in the eye of an observer", from competing behaviours. Hypothesis: representation is the wrong unit of abstraction for the bulk of intelligence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-351](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-351.md)) from the copy Brooks posts; worth reading as the decomposition side built and run: a robot whose purposive behaviour comes from parallel layers of simple finite-state machines with no central representation and no central control, which Brooks likens to Minsky's account of human behaviour. The coherence of the whole, he says, exists "in the eye of an observer". The evidence is three layers on one physical robot, described rather than measured. It makes no claim about minds or experience and disclaims interest in the philosophy. |
| [LIT-577](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-577.md) | Sophisticated Inference | Friston, Da Costa, Hafner, Hesp & Parr (2021; arXiv 2020), Neural Computation 33(3):713–763. Ordinary active inference scores a fixed set of policies by expected free energy (risk plus ambiguity). Sophisticated inference instead evaluates the expected free energy of the next action recursively, averaging over the beliefs the agent would hold after each plausible outcome and action, which amounts to a tree search over belief states pruned below a probability of 1/16. In simulations it plans past short-term costs: a rat visits a mildly aversive cue, and a horizon of four escapes a local minimum in a maze. It recovers Bayes-adaptive RL in the zero-temperature limit. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-454](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-454.md)), from the arXiv preprint, whose displayed equations did not survive text extraction. Worth reading as the active-inference planning scheme the record's free-energy holdings otherwise lack: expected free energy evaluated recursively over future belief states, a deep tree search pruned by probability, with the Bellman equation as its formal analogue. The evidence is small simulations (a T-maze rat and an 8 × 8 grid). Flagged anthology-candidate: it is a planning algorithm, compared with reinforcement learning, and the anthology's agents-and-environments topic may hold it. |
| [LIT-607](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-607.md) | Natural Gradient Works Efficiently in Learning | Amari (1998), Neural Computation 10(2):251–276. When the parameter space carries a Riemannian metric G, the steepest descent direction of a loss is the natural gradient G⁻¹∇L, not the ordinary gradient. For a statistical model the metric is the Fisher information, the only invariant one. Online natural gradient learning with step 1/t is Fisher efficient: it attains the Cramér–Rao bound asymptotically, as well as the best batch estimator. The paper computes the metric and its inverse for a simple perceptron, for the group of nonsingular matrices (blind source separation, giving the update ∇L·WᵀW) and for linear systems, proposes an adaptive learning rate with 1/t convergence, and conjectures that the natural gradient escapes the plateaus of backpropagation. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-472](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-472.md)); worth reading as the source of the natural gradient: steepest descent in a Riemannian parameter space is G⁻¹∇L (Theorem 1), the Fisher information is the metric on a statistical model, and online learning with the natural gradient and a 1/t rate is Fisher efficient (Theorem 2). Its efficiency proof needs the Fisher matrix at the optimum to be invertible, which is exactly what singular learning theory says fails for neural networks. |
| [LIT-608](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-608.md) | Deep Equals Shallow for ReLU Networks in Kernel Regimes | Bietti & Bach (2021), ICLR 2021. Dot-product kernels on the sphere are diagonal in spherical harmonics, with one eigenvalue µ_k per degree k shared by N(d, k) ~ k^(d−2) harmonics. Theorem 1 reads the asymptotic decay of µ_k off the kernel function's expansion at ±1: a non-integer exponent ν there gives µ_k ~ k^(−d−2ν+1). The arc-cosine kernels have ν = 1/2 and 3/2, and composing them preserves ν, so the NTK of a deep ReLU network decays as k^(−d) and its random-feature kernel as k^(−d−2), exactly as for two layers. Deep and shallow ReLU kernels therefore have the same RKHS, the same as the Laplace kernel's for the NTK. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-475](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-475.md)): main text and Appendix A in full, the proofs in Appendices B and C followed at the level of their lemmas. Worth reading as the general rule behind the NTK eigenvalue decays the record holds: for a dot-product kernel on the sphere, the decay of its spherical-harmonic eigenvalues is fixed by the kernel function's non-integer exponent at the endpoints ±1 (Theorem 1). Deep ReLU kernels keep the shallow exponent, so depth leaves the spectrum's shape unchanged: µ_k ~ C(d, L) k^(−d) for the NTK and k^(−d−2) for the random-feature kernel, with only the constant growing in L (Corollaries 2–3). |
| [LIT-611](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-611.md) | Gemma Scope: Open Sparse Autoencoders Everywhere All At Once on Gemma 2 | Lieberum et al. (2024), Google DeepMind technical report. Gemma Scope releases JumpReLU sparse autoencoders trained on the attention, MLP and residual-stream activations of every layer of Gemma 2 2B and 9B, and of three layers of 27B: over 400 SAEs, over 2,000 counting sparsity variants, and over 30 million latents. Each latent fires only above a learned threshold θ_i, and training penalises the L0 count of active latents directly, through straight-through estimators. Evaluation is by sparsity–fidelity curves (delta LM loss and FVU against mean L0). Base-model SAEs transfer to the instruction-tuned model, wider SAEs split latents, and the authors state that no agreed metric of SAE quality exists. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-482](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-482.md)). Worth reading as the technical report for the open SAE suite that later SAE studies, including the anthology's, are run on, and as the clearest statement of what a JumpReLU SAE is. A JumpReLU SAE is a learned hard threshold per latent, z ⊙ H(z − θ), trained against squared reconstruction error plus λ‖f(x)‖₀ (Eqs. 3–4). The report releases over 400 such SAEs (over 2,000 counting the sparsity variants) on every layer and sublayer of Gemma 2 2B and 9B and on three layers of 27B. Its evaluations are sparsity–fidelity curves, with no criterion offered for choosing a width or a sparsity; the authors say there is no consensus on what measures SAE quality. |
| [LIT-612](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-612.md) | The Convergence Rate of Neural Networks for Learned Functions of Different Frequencies | Basri, Jacobs, Kasten & Kritchman (2019), NeurIPS 2019. In the linearised dynamics of a wide two-layer ReLU network, on uniform data on a sphere, the Gram matrix H∞ is a convolution, so its eigenvectors are Fourier modes or spherical harmonics. Its eigenvalues are computed in closed form per frequency. Without bias, every odd frequency k ≥ 3 has eigenvalue zero, so the network cannot represent or learn it (Theorems 2 and 4). With a zero-initialised bias all frequencies pass. The eigenvalues fall as 1/k² on S¹ and, numerically, about 1/k^(d+1) on S^d, so the time to learn frequency k grows as k² and k³ on the circle and the 2-sphere. Deep and residual networks show the same exponents. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-481](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-481.md)): main text in full, the supplementary derivations of the S^d eigenvalues skimmed. Worth reading for the closed-form NTK eigenvalues per frequency and the exact null space they reveal. On the circle the bias-free two-layer ReLU kernel has eigenvalue 2(k²+1)/(π²(k²−1)²) on even k ≥ 2 and exactly zero on odd k ≥ 3 (Eq. 12), so such a network cannot represent cos 3θ at all (Theorems 2 and 4). A zero-initialised bias fills the null space, with 1/(π²k²) on odd k (Eq. 13). Convergence time then grows as k² on S¹ and about k³ on S², and shallow, deep and residual networks match: fitted exponents 1.93–2.15 on S¹ and 2.74–3.13 on S² (Figs. 6–7). |
| [LIT-613](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-613.md) | Traces of Class/Cross-Class Structure Pervade Deep Learning Spectra | Papyan (2020), JMLR 21(252). Cross-entropy indexes every deepnet quantity by example, class and would-be class, a two-way MANOVA layout. In the spectra of features, backpropagated errors, gradients, the Fisher, the Hessian and weights, knockouts attribute the top outlier to the global mean, C−1 outliers to between-class second moment, a mini-bulk of C(C−1) to between-cross-class covariance, and the main bulk to within-cross-class covariance. Feature and error class means separate from the bulk and become orthogonal with depth. Gradient class means are approximately feature class means ⊗ error class means, layer by layer; K-FAC's single Kronecker product misaligns the Fisher's outliers and the class-wise CFAC aligns them. For multinomial logistic regression on a Gaussian class model the expected Fisher spectrum is derived exactly. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-474](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-474.md)); worth reading as the general account of class/cross-class structure in deepnet spectra: features, backpropagated errors, gradients, Fisher, Hessian and weights all show one outlier from the global mean, C−1 from class means, a mini-bulk of about C(C−1) from cross-class means, and a main bulk from within-class variation. Per layer, gradient class means are approximately Kronecker products of feature class means and error class means, which is why K-FAC, pairing every class with every class, misaligns the Fisher's outliers, and CFAC, pairing each class with itself, aligns them. Proved only for multinomial logistic regression on a Gaussian model. |
| [LIT-616](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-616.md) | A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion | Watanabe (2012), arXiv:1208.6338; JMLR 14:867–897 (2013). A model is singular when the parameter-to-distribution map is not one-to-one or the Fisher information is not positive definite: neural networks, mixtures, reduced-rank regression, HMMs. Its Bayes free energy is nL_n(w0) + λ log n − (m − 1) log log n + O_p(1), with λ the real log canonical threshold (RLCT), not d/2. WBIC, the posterior average of nL_n(w) at inverse temperature 1/log n, has the same leading terms even for singular, unrealizable models, equals BIC for regular ones, and needs no knowledge of the true distribution. Two temperatures give an estimate of λ. In reduced-rank regression WBIC picked the true rank in 100 of 100 trials and recovered theoretical RLCTs closely. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-473](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-473.md)); worth reading as the record's lawful, short statement of the core of singular learning theory, standing in for Watanabe's unread book ([LIT-354](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-354.md)). It states the Bayes free energy asymptotics F = nL_n(w0) + λ log n − (m − 1) log log n + O_p(1), with λ the real log canonical threshold and m its multiplicity (Theorem 2), and defines λ through resolution of singularities (Theorem 1, Eq. 18). Its own result is WBIC, the posterior mean of nL_n(w) at inverse temperature 1/log n, which matches F to the λ log n term even for singular and unrealizable models (Theorem 4), equals BIC for regular ones (Theorem 5), and estimates λ from two temperatures (Corollary 3). The prior results are stated with citations to the book, not re-proved. |
| [LIT-617](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-617.md) | The Full Spectrum of Deepnet Hessians at Scale: Dynamics with SGD Training and Sample Size | Papyan (2018), arXiv. Stochastic Lanczos without reorthogonalization (O(Mnp) time, O(p) memory) plus subspace-iteration deflation measures the full Hessian spectrum of VGG11 and ResNet18 on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10/100, over 16,000 trained models. It confirms a bulk with about C outliers, attributes the outliers to the Gauss–Newton term G and most of the bulk to the residual H, finds H's spectrum symmetric with a power-law tail rather than Marchenko–Pastur, and finds H never negligible. Version 2 decomposes G into class means (outliers), cross-class variation and within-class variation (two bulks) and tracks them across epochs and sample sizes. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-478](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-478.md)); worth reading as the measurement that the bulk-and-C-outliers spectrum of the Hessian persists at full scale (VGG11, 28M parameters), that the outliers belong to the Gauss–Newton/Fisher term G and the bulk mostly to the residual H, and, in its second version, that G splits into class means (outliers) and two bulks (cross-class and within-class variation). Its tools are stochastic Lanczos spectral density estimation without reorthogonalization, plus subspace-iteration deflation. |
| [LIT-618](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-618.md) | Prevalence of Neural Collapse during the terminal phase of deep learning training | Papyan, Han & Donoho (2020), PNAS 117(40). Training past zero error (the terminal phase, TPT) drives four linked phenomena in the last layer: within-class variability collapses (Tr(Σ_WΣ_B†)/C → 0), centred class means become equinorm and equiangular with cosines −1/(C−1), a simplex ETF; classifier rows become proportional to the means; and the decision becomes nearest class mean. Measured on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, STL10 and ImageNet with VGG, ResNet and DenseNet, 480 models. Test accuracy and DeepFool robustness keep improving during TPT. Theorems: NC1–NC2 imply NC3–NC4 for the Webb–Lowe and Soudry max-margin classifiers, and the simplex ETF uniquely maximizes the small-noise error exponent. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-476](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-476.md)); worth reading as the source of neural collapse: in the terminal phase of training, last-layer features collapse to their class means (NC1), the centred means form a simplex equiangular tight frame (NC2), the classifier aligns with them (NC3) and the decision becomes nearest class centre (NC4). Measured on 7 datasets × 3 architectures; NC1–NC2 imply NC3–NC4 for the Webb–Lowe and max-margin classifiers, and the simplex ETF is the unique optimal codebook in a vanishing-noise Gaussian channel. It explains Papyan's Hessian outliers as class means outgrowing collapsing within-class variation. |
| [LIT-619](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-619.md) | Measurements of Three-Level Hierarchical Structure in the Outliers in the Spectrum of Deepnet Hessians | Papyan (2019), ICML. For a C-class network the Gauss–Newton term of the Hessian is G = (1/n)ΔΔᵀ, a second moment (not covariance) of logit derivatives δᵢ,c,c′ indexed by example, true class and logit. Grouping them into C² group means δc,c′ and C clusters with centres δc gives G = G₀ + G₁ + G₂ + G₃ (Eq. 28). The top-C outliers of G are those of G₁ = (C−1)Ave_c δcδcᵀ, because clusters are far apart and tight. Early in training the group means cluster by logit c′, later by true class c. Holds across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet with VGG, ResNet and DenseNet; the outliers exceed their approximations slightly, as random matrix theory would predict. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-479](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-479.md)); worth reading as the paper that explains the C outliers of the deepnet Hessian: the Gauss–Newton/Fisher term G is a second moment, not a covariance, of logit derivatives indexed by (example, class, logit), and the C outliers are the eigenvalues of G₁ = (C−1)·Ave_c δ_c δ_cᵀ, the C class-cluster centres, computable from a C×C Gram matrix without high-dimensional eigenanalysis. The match is empirical, over 18,000 trained models. |
| [LIT-621](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-621.md) | Shampoo: Preconditioned Stochastic Tensor Optimization | Gupta, Koren & Singer (2018), ICML. For a parameter tensor of order k, Shampoo keeps one preconditioner per dimension, each the gradient contracted with itself over all other dimensions, and multiplies the gradient along dimension i by (Hⁱ)^{-1/2k}. In the matrix case this is W ← W − η L^{-1/4} G R^{-1/4}, equivalent to preconditioning the flattened gradient by (L ⊗ R)^{1/4}, which upper-bounds the full-matrix AdaGrad preconditioner up to the gradient rank (Lemma 8). Regret is O(√T) in online convex optimization (Theorems 7, 10). On CIFAR-10/100 and LM1B it converges faster than SGD with momentum, Adam and AdaGrad at similar step time. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-480](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-480.md)); worth reading as the source of per-dimension Kronecker preconditioning: for a matrix parameter, left and right statistics L = Σ GGᵀ and R = Σ GᵀG, update W ← W − η L^{-1/4} G R^{-1/4}, i.e. a step preconditioned by (L ⊗ R)^{1/4}, which by Lemma 8 dominates the full AdaGrad matrix. Its statistic is the accumulated gradient outer product, not the Fisher; its guarantee is an O(√T) regret in online convex optimization; its deep-learning evidence is four training curves. |
| [LIT-622](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-622.md) | Optimizing Neural Networks with Kronecker-factored Approximate Curvature | Martens & Grosse (2015), ICML. K-FAC approximates natural gradient descent in neural networks. Each Fisher block between layers i and j, E[āᵢ₋₁āⱼ₋₁ᵀ ⊗ gᵢgⱼᵀ], is replaced by E[āᵢ₋₁āⱼ₋₁ᵀ] ⊗ E[gᵢgⱼᵀ] (activations times backpropagated derivatives), whose error is a sum of third- and fourth-order cumulants. The inverse is then taken as block-diagonal or block-tridiagonal across layers. With factored Tikhonov damping, re-scaling by the exact Fisher, an adaptive momentum and a growing mini-batch, it needs orders of magnitude fewer iterations than tuned SGD with Nesterov momentum on three deep autoencoder benchmarks, and it is invariant to affine reparameterizations of each layer's inputs and pre-activations. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-486](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-486.md)); worth reading as the source of the Kronecker-factored Fisher: each layer's Fisher block E[āāᵀ ⊗ ggᵀ] is approximated by E[āāᵀ] ⊗ E[ggᵀ], so it inverts as two small matrices, and the inverse is further taken as block-diagonal or block-tridiagonal across layers. The factorization is justified by small higher-order cumulants, checked on one small tanh network; the speedups are on three deep autoencoders. |
| [LIT-623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-623.md) v2 | Bayesian Interpolation | MacKay (1992), Neural Computation 4(3):415–447. Two levels of inference: fit each model, then rank models by their evidence P(D\|H). Under a Gaussian approximation the evidence is the best-fit likelihood times an Occam factor, the ratio of posterior to prior accessible parameter volume, so complex or finely tuned models penalise themselves (Eqs. 5–6). For linear interpolation with quadratic regularisers the evidence sets the regularising constant and the noise level through γ, the number of well-determined parameters (2αE_W = γ, 2βE_D = N − γ). It ranks polynomial, radial-basis, spline, Hermite and neural-network models on two data sets. In expectation, no fixed model's log evidence beats the true model's. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-471](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-471.md)); worth reading as the source of the evidence framework and the Occam factor in the form the field uses: evidence ≈ best-fit likelihood × Occam factor, the Occam factor being the ratio of posterior to prior accessible parameter volume, (2π)^{k/2} det^{-1/2}A · P(w_MP\|H) under a Gaussian approximation (Eqs. 5–6). It also gives the "number of good parameter measurements" γ = Σ λ_a/(λ_a + α), which sets the regularising constant (2αE_W = γ) and the noise level (2βE_D = N − γ) at the evidence maximum. The framework is Gull and Skilling's, as MacKay says, and every demonstration is one-dimensional interpolation. Flagged anthology-candidate for its regularisation and early-stopping arguments. |
| [LIT-624](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-624.md) | Towards Understanding the Spectral Bias of Deep Learning | Cao, Fang, Wu, Zhou & Gu (2019). For a two-layer ReLU network trained by gradient descent on squared loss, the training residual projected onto the eigenfunctions of the NTK integral operator with the r_k largest eigenvalues decays like (1 − λ_(r_k))^T (Theorem 4.2). This holds for any labelling, provided the sample size beats the eigengap and the width is polynomial in λ_(r_k)^(−1). On uniform data on S^d the eigenfunctions are spherical harmonics, with µ_k = Ω(k^(−d−1)) for k ≫ d and Ω(d^(−k+1)) for d ≫ k on even degrees, and µ_k = 0 on odd k ≥ 3 (Theorem 4.3). Lower degrees are learned first, faster, and with fewer samples and narrower networks. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-483](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-483.md)): main text and Appendix A in full, the proofs in Appendix B followed at the level of their lemmas. Worth reading as the theorem that makes "spectral bias" a statement about NTK eigendirections: for a two-layer ReLU network trained by gradient descent, the residual projected onto the top r_k eigenfunctions of the NTK integral operator shrinks like (1 − λ_(r_k))^T (Theorem 4.2), for any target, with sample size governed by the eigengap λ_(r_k) − λ_(r_k+1). On uniform spherical data the eigenfunctions are spherical harmonics, the odd degrees above 1 have eigenvalue zero, and µ_k = Ω(max(k^(−d−1), d^(−k+1))) for even k (Theorem 4.3). |
| [LIT-642](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-642.md) | Psychologism and Behaviorism | Block (1981), The Philosophical Review 90(1):5–43. Psychologism, the doctrine that whether behaviour is intelligent depends on the information processing that produces it, is true. A machine that stores all sensible conversations of a test's length and looks up its replies has the capacity to respond sensibly to any sequence of inputs, so it satisfies the strongest behaviourist conception of intelligence, yet all its intelligence is its programmers'. The standard objections to behaviourism (Chisholm–Geach, the perfect actor, paralytics) defeat behaviourist necessary conditions but not sufficient ones; this machine defeats the sufficient condition. Psychologism is not chauvinism: it excludes one kind of processing without requiring ours. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-506](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-506.md)); worth reading as the source of the "Blockhead": a machine that stores every sensible hour-long conversation and so has the capacity to pass any Turing test of that length, yet "has the intelligence of a toaster". The argument refutes behaviourist sufficient conditions for intelligence, including a capacity version that survives the standard objections, and establishes psychologism: whether behaviour is intelligent depends partly on the processing that produces it. It does not say which processing is required, only that it needs some "richness", and the closing case against simulators of physics, neurons or psychology is admitted to be a sketch. |
| [LIT-651](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-651.md) | Linear Mode Connectivity in Multitask and Continual Learning | Mirzadeh, Farajtabar, Gorur, Pascanu & Ghasemzadeh (2020). When a multitask solution and a continual solution start from the same point, the multitask solution lies on a low-loss line to every earlier continual solution, while consecutive continual solutions are separated by rising loss. Euclidean distance and CKA do not detect the difference. The multitask direction lies outside the top Hessian eigenvectors of the earlier task. MC-SGD trains towards a point linearly connected to both the previous solution and the current task's solution, using a small replay buffer, and leads five baselines on three 20-task benchmarks. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-520](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-520.md)); worth reading as the first study of where continual and multitask solutions lie relative to each other. Started from the same point (the previous task's solution), the multitask solution is linearly connected with low loss to every earlier continual solution, while consecutive continual solutions are not. The authors explain it by curvature: the multitask path moves in directions the earlier task's Hessian sees as flat, within a region where a second-order expansion holds. MC-SGD turns this into a regulariser and beats EWC, A-GEM, ER-Reservoir and Stable SGD on 20-task Permuted MNIST, Rotated MNIST and Split CIFAR-100. The connectivity breaks with a different start, input noise, label corruption or removed classes. |
| [LIT-652](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-652.md) | The Role of Permutation Invariance in Linear Mode Connectivity of Neural Networks | Entezari, Sedghi, Saukh & Neyshabur (2022), ICLR 2022. Conjecture: most SGD solutions lie in a set whose members can be permuted so that no barrier remains on the line between any two. Barriers between networks from different initializations first rise then fall with width, rise with depth, and saturate high for VGGs and ResNets. A proof covers a wide one-hidden-layer net at uniform random initialization. The evidence is a model: random permutations of one SGD solution show the same barriers as independent solutions across width, depth and dataset. A simulated annealing search lowers barriers only for shallow networks. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-537](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-537.md)); the source of the conjecture that SGD solutions, once their hidden units are suitably permuted, have no barrier on the straight line between them: one basin modulo permutation. Its proof covers only a one-hidden-layer network at uniform random initialization, and its main evidence is indirect: barriers between independently trained networks behave like barriers between random permutations of a single trained network, across width, depth and dataset, in more than 3,000 networks. Its own permutation search lowers barriers only for shallow nets on easy data and fails for VGGs and ResNets. Second reading under [ADR-013](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-013.md); the anthology holds it as [ANTH-LIT-251](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/blob/main/record/literature.d/LIT-251.md), and that entry misstates the theorem. |
| [LIT-653](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-653.md) | Essentially No Barriers in Neural Network Energy Landscape | Draxler, Veschgini, Salmhofer & Hamprecht (2018), ICML 2018. Using AutoNEB, a minimum-energy-path method from molecular statistical mechanics, the paper connects ten minima per architecture for CNNs, ResNets and DenseNets on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The saddle losses on the best paths are almost those of the minima for deep architectures, and test error rises by at most a few tenths of a percent on CIFAR-10. The conclusion is that minima are points on one connected low-loss manifold, not bottoms of separate valleys, and that the effect grows with width and especially depth. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-531](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-531.md)); the other founding demonstration of mode connectivity, reached independently of Garipov et al. by borrowing the nudged elastic band from chemical physics. Over ten minima per architecture, the highest training loss on the best paths found is almost the minima's own for deep ResNets and DenseNets on CIFAR-10, with a small residual gap on CIFAR-100, and barriers fall as networks get wider and especially deeper. Its two explanations, resilience and redundancy, are qualitative; the redundancy toy (swapping two hidden units needs a third) is the first statement in this batch of why a permutation costs a barrier without spare capacity. |
| [LIT-654](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-654.md) | Linear Mode Connectivity and the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis | Frankle, Dziugaite, Roy & Carbin (2020), ICML 2020. Instability analysis trains two copies of a network from the same state under different SGD noise and measures the error barrier on the straight line between the results. Standard vision networks are unstable at initialization but become stable early in training, after which the outcome is fixed to one linearly connected minimum. Sparse subnetworks found by iterative magnitude pruning reach full accuracy only when they are stable, which explains where lottery tickets were and were not found, and rewinding to an early iterate rather than to initialization finds matching subnetworks at ImageNet scale. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-514](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-514.md)); the source of linear mode connectivity as a measurement and of instability analysis. Two copies of a network trained from the same state under different SGD noise end up linearly connected once that state is a little way into training (3% for ResNet-20, 20% for ResNet-50 on ImageNet), and iterative-magnitude-pruning subnetworks are matching only when they are stable in this sense. The evidence is correlational: stability and matching coincide across the settings tested, and nothing shows that one causes the other. |
| [LIT-655](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-655.md) | Understanding Mode Connectivity via Parameter Space Symmetry | Zhao, Dehmamy, Walters & Yu (2025), ICML 2025. Relates the topology of a loss's symmetry group to that of its minimum. The minimum of a full-rank l-layer linear regression is homeomorphic to GL_h(ℝ)^{l−1}, so it has 2^{l−1} components; a skip connection reduces 4 to 3 in a 1-D case, and permutations connect all components when h ≥ 2. Rescaling symmetry yields minima in one component with arbitrarily large barriers on the straight line. Group actions give explicit constant-loss curves, and a curvature bound κ on such a curve bounds the chord's distance from the minimum by about κ‖w₂ − w₁‖²/8. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-528](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-528.md)); worth reading as the account of mode connectivity from continuous parameter symmetries. The minimum of a full-rank l-layer linear network is homeomorphic to GL_h(ℝ)^{l−1} and so has 2^{l−1} connected components, a skip connection merges some of them, and a permutation with negative determinant joins the rest. Rescaling symmetry gives minima in the same component with an arbitrarily large loss barrier on the straight line between them, even after a restricted permutation. A group element g gives an explicit constant-loss curve exp(t log g)·w, and bounded curvature of such curves bounds the barrier on the chord. The theory is for linear networks and homogeneous last layers; the experiments are small synthetic regressions. |
| [LIT-656](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-656.md) | Loss Surface Simplexes for Mode Connecting Volumes and Fast Ensembling | Benton, Maddox, Lotfi & Wilson (2021), ICML 2021. SPRO trains the connecting vertices of simplexes so that loss is low at points sampled uniformly inside them, with a log-volume bonus. It finds simplicial complexes of low loss joining up to seven independently trained networks through shared vertices, and a low-loss region around VGG-16 on CIFAR-10 of at least 10 dimensions. Started from a single trained network, a few vertices cost about a tenth of a training run each, and ensembling inside the simplexes (ESPRO) beats deep ensembles in accuracy, calibration and robustness to corruption. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-539](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-539.md)); mode connectivity raised from curves to volumes. Training the vertices of simplexes so that loss stays low at random points inside them finds simplicial complexes of low loss joining several independently trained networks at once, and a low-loss region around a VGG-16 on CIFAR-10 of at least 10 dimensions. The same trick, run from one trained network, gives cheap ensembles (ESPRO) that beat deep ensembles at equal size and budget. The dimension estimate is a lower bound from one architecture and dataset, and the paper's picture of one connected volume containing all SGD solutions is drawn from complexes of up to 7 modes. |
| [LIT-657](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-657.md) | The Generalization Ridge: Information Flow in Natural Language Generation | Chang, Deng & Chen (2025), COLM 2026. InfoRidge estimates, layer by layer and through fine-tuning, the matrix-based mutual information between a transformer's last-token hidden state and the embedding of the target token, and between each block's residual update and that target. In GPT-2 Small and Medium, Qwen-2.5 0.5B and Llama 3.1 8B on CLUTRR, ECQA and a synthetic arithmetic task, it rises, peaks in the upper-middle layers and falls. On the synthetic task the peak coincides with the best OOD early-exit accuracy while ID accuracy keeps rising. Middle blocks add the most information, attention to task tokens peaks there, and residual scales fitted on OOD data downweight the last layers. The profile persists over 50 decoding steps on CNN/DailyMail. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-536](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-536.md)); worth reading as a layer-wise information profile of fine-tuned language models: a matrix-based Rényi estimate of I(Zℓ; Y), between the last-token hidden state at layer ℓ and the input embedding of the true next token, rises through the early layers, peaks in the upper-middle layers and falls in the last few, the "generalization ridge". On a synthetic arithmetic task with GPT-2 Small the peak (0.27 at layer 10 of 12) is where OOD early-exit accuracy is best (56.9%) while ID accuracy keeps rising to 93.2% at layer 12. Learned residual scales put less weight on the final layers when fitted on OOD data. The estimator is a kernel-alignment quantity, not Shannon mutual information: at layer 12 it falls to 0.019, near its layer-6 value, where the same layer decodes the target with 93% ID accuracy. |
| [LIT-658](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-658.md) | Knowledge is a Region in Weight Space for Fine-tuned Language Models | Gueta, Venezian, Raffel, Slonim, Katz & Choshen (2023). RoBERTa-base models fine-tuned on similar data end up close in weight space: task vectors cluster by dataset (98% clustering accuracy over 280 models) and by task family (90%), and the grouping follows data type, not data size. Points between the fine-tuned models, along lines and across their convex hull, perform as well or better than the fine-tuned models themselves, and linear extrapolation beyond them quickly fails. The region's centroid, re-fine-tuned with BitFit, beats starting from the pretrained model on 9 of 12 target datasets. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-515](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-515.md)); worth reading as the paper that turns linear connectivity between fine-tuned models into a claim about regions. RoBERTa-base models fine-tuned on the same dataset, the same task, or any of 12 GLUE/SuperGLUE datasets cluster in weight space by cosine of their task vectors, and the convex hull of each group performs as well as or better than the fine-tuned members: sampled hull points beat the members in 88% of comparisons on MNLI. Linear extrapolation past the members fails quickly, so the fine-tuned models sit near the edge of a small basin. Averaging the region (its centroid) is a better start for further fine-tuning than the pretrained model on 9 of 12 datasets. One pretrained model, classification only, English only. |
| [LIT-659](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-659.md) | Do Deep Neural Network Solutions Form a Star Domain? | Sonthalia, Rubinstein, Abbasnejad & Oh (2024), preprint. Conjectures that SGD solution sets, modulo permutation, are star domains, which needs less width than convexity does. Starlight trains a star model by sampling points on the lines to permuted source models. The star model has much lower loss barriers to held-out solutions than those solutions have to each other, across ResNet-18, VGG, DenseNet, CIFAR and ImageNet-1k (e.g. 0.078 against 0.383 on CIFAR-10). It gains with more source models, ranks uncertainty better in BMA than a deep ensemble, and is about 1 point more accurate than a single model. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-533](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-533.md)); worth reading as the star domain conjecture: where SGD solutions are not convex modulo permutation, they still form a star domain, with a star model linearly connected, after weight matching, to every other solution. Starlight trains a candidate by sampling points on the lines to 50 permuted source models, and the candidate has lower barriers to held-out models than those models have to each other (ResNet-18 CIFAR-10 0.078 against 0.383; ImageNet-1k 2.794 against 5.948). Those barriers are lower, not zero, and the authors say the conjecture is unproved and the barriers are often significantly above zero. Preprint. |
| [LIT-660](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-660.md) | Mode Connectivity Beyond Classifiers: Evidence from Generative and Contrastive Models | Yao, Zhang & Tian (2026), preprint. Extends layer-wise path construction (LLPF, Tian et al. 2026) to a DDPM on Flowers102 and a NanoCLIP model on Flickr30k. Layers move towards the target mode in a dataflow order (symmetric encoder–decoder pairs for the U-Net, alternating vision and text blocks for CLIP); each layer is rescaled to a fixed variance; the point is retrained with AdamW until its loss is below a threshold. The resulting chains keep training loss below 0.04 (DDPM) and 0.09 (NanoCLIP), where AutoNEB's maximum NanoCLIP loss is 6.69. Intermediate DDPMs have worse FID than the endpoints at equal training loss. | Proposed — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-534](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-534.md)); watching, as the first claim of mode connectivity between independently trained generative and contrastive models: one pair of DDPMs on Flowers102 and one pair of NanoCLIP models on Flickr30k, joined by a chain of checkpoints along which the training loss stays below a threshold, where AutoNEB's paths rise steeply on NanoCLIP. The path is built by moving layer groups towards the far end, rescaling each layer's variance, and retraining with AdamW until the loss is under threshold, so every anchor is a retrained model. What would settle it: more than one pair per model, a barrier measure along the whole path rather than at the anchors, and a reason to think a path made of retrained anchors says more about the landscape than that retraining works. It is a preprint of 31 August 2026. |
| [LIT-661](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-661.md) | Git Re-Basin: Merging Models modulo Permutation Symmetries | Ainsworth, Hayase & Srinivasa (2023), ICLR 2023. Three ways to permute one network's hidden units into alignment with another: activation matching (a linear assignment per layer), weight matching (an NP-hard sum of bilinear assignments, solved by coordinate descent over layers), and a straight-through estimator. After alignment the straight line between independently trained networks has zero loss barrier for MLPs on MNIST and wide ResNet-20s on CIFAR-10. Connectivity grows with width and with training time, fails for thin models, and a counterexample shows it is a property of SGD solutions. Merging models trained on disjoint data improves test loss and calibration but not accuracy. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-532](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-532.md)); the strongest evidence for one basin modulo permutation. A weight-matching algorithm that needs no data and runs in seconds aligns independently trained networks so that the straight line between them has no loss barrier, for MLPs on MNIST and for ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 at large width, the first such result for ResNets. It also finds where the picture stops: thin models are not linearly connected after any permutation it finds, connectivity appears only after some training, ImageNet ResNet-50 keeps a barrier, and a constructed counterexample shows that the property belongs to SGD solutions, not to architectures. Second reading under [ADR-013](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-013.md); the anthology holds it as [ANTH-LIT-333](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/blob/main/record/literature.d/LIT-333.md), and that entry misdescribes the algorithm and overstates the results. |
| [LIT-662](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-662.md) | Geodesic Mode Connectivity | Tan, Long, Zhao & Laine (2023), ICLR 2023 Tiny Paper. Treats a network as a distribution p(x, ŷ; θ) on a Fisher–Rao manifold and hypothesises that geodesics between SGD solutions are mode-connecting paths. A chain of 25 models between two ResNet-20s (4× width, LayerNorm), initialised on the straight line after Git Re-Basin weight matching, is optimised to minimise summed Jensen–Shannon divergence between neighbours. The curve is longer in Euclidean terms but shorter in distribution space, and keeps train and test loss low where linear interpolation shows a large barrier. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-521](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-521.md)); worth reading as the short proposal that mode-connecting paths are geodesics of the Fisher–Rao metric on the space of the networks' output distributions. It approximates a geodesic between two trained ResNet-20s (4× width, LayerNorm), after Git Re-Basin weight matching, by optimising 25 models on a chain to minimise the summed Jensen–Shannon divergence between neighbours, using unlabelled training images only, and the resulting curve has low train and test loss where the straight line does not. One architecture, one pair, one figure; the hypothesis that all geodesics between SGD solutions are mode-connecting is stated, not tested. |
| [LIT-663](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-663.md) | Taxonomizing local versus global structure in neural network loss landscapes | Yang, Hodgkinson, Theisen, Zou, Gonzalez, Ramchandran & Mahoney (2021), NeurIPS. Thousands of trained networks are placed on a load-like by temperature-like grid and measured three ways: Hessian top eigenvalue and trace (local sharpness), Bezier-curve mode connectivity between two independently trained models (global connectivity), and CKA similarity of their outputs on mixup points. Two transitions give four phases: I sharp and poorly connected, II sharp and well connected, III flat and poorly connected, IV flat and well connected, with IV split by CKA into IV-A and IV-B. Test accuracy is best in IV-B. Sharpness alone mispredicts accuracy across phases, and in phase III training to zero loss does worse than stopping in the sharp phases. Double descent appears as a dark band at the phase boundary under label noise. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-516](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-516.md)); worth reading as the empirical taxonomy of loss landscapes by local and global structure: Hessian top eigenvalue and trace separate locally sharp from locally flat, Bezier-curve mode connectivity between independently trained models separates globally poorly-connected from well-connected, and CKA similarity of their outputs splits the well-connected, flat phase in two. Across a load-like by temperature-like grid (width, data amount or label noise against batch size, learning rate or weight decay), the best test accuracy sits in the flat, well-connected, high-similarity phase IV-B; the Hessian alone mispredicts, and where connectivity is poor, training to zero loss can lower test accuracy. Empirical only, mostly ResNet18 on CIFAR-10. |
| [LIT-664](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-664.md) | Generalized Linear Mode Connectivity for Transformers | Theus, Cabodi, Anagnostidis, Orvieto, Singh & Boeva (2025), NeurIPS 2025. A hierarchy of function-preserving maps (permutation ⊂ semi-permutation ⊂ orthogonal ⊂ invertible) fits transformer components: permutations for feed-forward units, semi-permutations for attention heads, an orthogonal map on the RMSNorm residual stream. Aligning with them gives, for the first time, low and zero test-loss barriers between independently trained ViTs and GPT-2s (learned matching 0.00 on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet, 0.02 Tiny Shakespeare, 0.42 BookCorpus), for three-way merges and across embedding widths. Permutation-only alignment does not get there. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-540](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-540.md)); worth reading as the result that independently trained transformers become linearly mode connected once alignment uses their real symmetries: permutations of feed-forward units, semi-permutations of attention heads, and an orthogonal map on the residual stream after RMSNorm reparameterisation. Data-free weight matching cuts test-loss barriers from 1.69–4.34 to 0.34–1.56, and learned matching, which optimises the alignment against task loss at the midpoint, reaches 0.00 on three vision datasets and 0.02 and 0.42 on two language ones. Most of the gap is in the orthogonal map. Small ViTs and GPT-2s only. |
| [LIT-665](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-665.md) | ZipIt! Merging Models from Different Tasks without Training | Stoica, Bolya, Bjorner, Ramesh, Hearn & Hoffman (2023), ICLR 2024. Merging differently initialised models trained on disjoint tasks fails under permutation, because the permuted model sits in a basin for its own task and not the other's. ZipIt! instead merges correlated features within and across models through merge and unmerge matrices, and can stop merging part-way, giving a shared trunk with task heads. The abstract reports a 20–60% improvement over prior work on CIFAR and ImageNet splits; it comes near the ensemble with partial zipping, and proves a tighter LMC barrier bound than Entezari et al. when units are redundant. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-523](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-523.md)), main text and Appendices A–F, the proof in Appendix G followed to its reduction to Entezari et al.; worth reading as the case that permutation is the wrong symmetry for merging models trained on different tasks. ZipIt! matches features by activation correlation within each model as well as across the two, and can stop merging at a chosen layer, leaving a multi-head model. On disjoint halves of CIFAR-10 it reaches 79.1% joint accuracy where Git Re-Basin reaches 46.2%, and partial zipping comes within a few points of the ensemble. Its theorem tightens Entezari et al.'s barrier bound when a model has redundant units. With full merging on ImageNet-1k it is no better than a permutation baseline (8.6%), so the gains there come from leaving later layers unmerged. |
| [LIT-666](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-666.md) | Mode Connectivity and Data Heterogeneity of Federated Learning | Zhou, Zhang & Tsang (2023), preprint. Under Dirichlet label skew and PACS domain shift, low-loss overlaps between FedAvg client models and the global model shrink as heterogeneity grows; client models stay close to the global one yet move in different directions within a round. Global models from one initialisation under different heterogeneity have function dissimilarity above 0.2, show an error barrier on the line, and are joined without barrier by a polygonal chain. A mean-field analysis of two-layer networks bounds dropout and connectivity errors by terms proportional to √h(α) and decreasing in width N. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-517](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-517.md)); worth reading as the only study in the batch of connectivity under federated averaging. Client models, though close in weight space, leave the low-loss region of the global model more as client data grow more heterogeneous, and FedAvg global models trained from one initialisation under different heterogeneity are separated on the straight line (accuracy drops of about 10%) but joined by a one-bend polygonal chain. A mean-field bound, extending the dropout-stability route of Kuditipudi et al. and Shevchenko and Mondelli, makes the connectivity error grow with √h(α), a heterogeneity factor, and shrink with width; width and heterogeneity trends in MNIST and CIFAR-10 runs agree. The theory treats heterogeneity as isotropic Gaussian noise on each neuron's update, an assumption the paper checks only by plotting noise norms. |
| [LIT-667](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-667.md) | Does Data Scaling Lead to Visual Compositional Generalization? | Uselis, Dittadi & Oh (2025), ICML 2025. Two labelled concepts with n values each form an n × n grid; training shows k combinations per value and testing uses the rest. On dSprites, 3DShapes, PUG, colored MNIST and a new FSprites, ResNet-50s trained from scratch reach near 100% on seen pairs and fall sharply on unseen ones; 4× more in-distribution data does not close the gap, while more values and more combinations do. Features pass from spurious, to discriminative but entangled, to linearly factored and near-orthogonal as combinatorial coverage grows. Exact linear factorization makes k = 2 sufficient for perfect generalization. Frozen DINO, DINOv2 and CLIP features are above chance but far from that ideal. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-525](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-525.md)); worth reading as a controlled test of whether more data buys visual compositional generalization: in an (n, k) grid where each of n values of two concepts is seen in only k combinations, ResNet-50s trained from scratch fail on unseen pairs whatever the data volume (4× more in-distribution data leaves 60–80% drops), and succeed only as the fraction of combinations seen rises, when their features become linearly factored (a pair's embedding is the sum of per-concept vectors; R² > 0.8). Under exact linear factorization, k = 2 combinations per value suffice for a linear classifier to get all unseen pairs right (Proposition 4.1). DINO, DINOv2 and CLIP features are partly factored. Model selection is oracle, on the test set, by design. |
| [LIT-668](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-668.md) | Bridging Mode Connectivity in Loss Landscapes and Adversarial Robustness | Zhao, Chen, Das, Ramamurthy & Lin (2020), ICLR 2020. A Garipov-style quadratic Bezier path between two tampered models, trained on a small clean set, contains models that keep clean accuracy and shed backdoor or injected-error attacks, outperforming fine-tuning, retraining, pruning and weight noise on the clean–attack trade-off in most settings. On a standard-loss path between a regular and an adversarially trained model, standard loss stays flat but robustness loss rises in the middle, and it correlates with the largest input-Hessian eigenvalue (Pearson 0.71–0.88). | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-530](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-530.md)); worth reading as the first use of mode connectivity for adversarial robustness. A quadratic Bezier path trained between two backdoored or error-injected models on as few as 50–2,500 clean samples contains models near its ends that keep most clean accuracy and lose the attack (CIFAR-10 VGG with 2,500 samples: 88% clean, 1.1% backdoor success at t = 0.1). Between a regular and an adversarially trained model, a path trained with the standard loss has no standard-loss barrier but a robustness-loss barrier, which tracks the largest eigenvalue of the input Hessian. The proposition offered for that correlation rests on an assumption that, taken literally, would rule out the barrier it explains. |
| [LIT-669](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-669.md) | Mechanistic Mode Connectivity | Lubana, Bigelow, Dick, Krueger & Tanaka (2022), ICML 2023. Two models are mechanistically similar if they are invariant to the same interventions on the data-generating process. Models that use a spurious cue and models that ignore it are mode connected along quadratic paths but not along linear ones, even after permutation matching, and the paper conjectures that a linear barrier implies mechanistic dissimilarity. For a one-hidden-layer ReLU network it proves only the converse: mechanisms of different complexity cannot be linearly connected. Naive fine-tuning on clean data stays linearly connected to the pretrained model and keeps its reliance on the cue; a fine-tune that forces a barrier removes it. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-538](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-538.md)); worth reading as the paper that ties a loss barrier to a difference in what two models compute. It defines two models as mechanistically similar when they are invariant to the same interventions on the data-generating process, finds that models relying on a spurious cue and models ignoring it are connected by quadratic paths but not by linear ones, even after permutation, and conjectures that a linear barrier always signals mechanistic dissimilarity. The conjecture is proved only for a one-hidden-layer ReLU network on a synthetic process; the evidence is synthetic cues on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Dominoes. |
| [LIT-670](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-670.md) | On Linear Mode Connectivity of Mixture-of-Experts Architectures | Tran, Trinh, Bui & Nguyen (2025), NeurIPS 2025. The group generated by permuting experts with their gates and translating all gating weights by a common vector preserves an MoE's function. Under genericity conditions it is the whole symmetry of the dense gate and of the top-k gate for k ≥ 2 (Theorems 4.1–4.2). Translation does not change barriers, so only the permutation matters. Matching expert order by centred gate weights or by Gram matrices, then weight-matching inside each expert, brings barriers between MoE layers fine-tuned from different seeds near zero, across dense, top-2 and DeepSeekMoE variants, on ViT and GPT-2 backbones that are shared and frozen. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-513](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-513.md)); worth reading as the characterisation of the symmetries of a mixture-of-experts gate. Under genericity conditions, two dense or top-k (k ≥ 2) MoEs compute the same function only if they differ by a permutation of experts together with their gates and a common translation of the gating weights (Theorems 4.1–4.2), and the translation leaves every barrier unchanged. Expert-order matching followed by per-expert weight matching gives near-zero barriers between MoE layers fine-tuned from different seeds. But the backbone around the MoE layer is shared and frozen, so what is connected is one inserted layer, not two independently trained networks. |
| [LIT-671](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-671.md) | Explaining Landscape Connectivity of Low-cost Solutions for Multilayer Nets | Kuditipudi, Wang, Lee, Zhang, Li, Hu, Arora & Ge (2019), NeurIPS 2019. Mode connectivity follows from generic robustness properties of trained nets. Two ε-dropout-stable ReLU networks, each able to zero half its units per layer at loss cost ε, are connected by a piecewise-linear path of loss at most max endpoint + ε; ε-noise-stable networks are connected by 10 segments with barrier Õ(ε). Conversely, for any width there is a dataset on which global minima of a two-layer student are disconnected, so connectivity is a property of the solutions training finds. Checked on MNIST convnets and VGG-11 on CIFAR-10. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-544](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-544.md)); the first explanation of mode connectivity that applies to realistic multilayer nets. If two solutions can each lose half their units per layer at a cost of at most ε in loss (dropout stability), they are joined by a piecewise-linear path whose loss never exceeds the worse endpoint by more than ε; a stronger noise-stability condition gives 10 segments. A counterexample shows that connectivity fails for some global minima of arbitrarily overparametrized two-layer nets, so the property belongs to the solutions training finds, not to the landscape. The conditions are checked on small MNIST convnets and one VGG-11 trained with channel-wise dropout. |
| [LIT-672](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-672.md) | Rethinking generalization requires revisiting old ideas: statistical mechanics approaches and complex learning behavior | Martin & Mahoney (2017), arXiv preprint. Zhang et al.'s observations, that deep networks fit noisy labels and that only early stopping regularizes them, are read through the statistical mechanics of learning. A Very Simple Deep Learning model has two control parameters: a load α = m_eff/N, lowered by randomizing labels, and a temperature τ, raised by stopping early. In the thermodynamic limit (m, N → ∞, α fixed), generalization error can drop discontinuously at a critical αc, and a two-dimensional (α, τ) phase diagram has a spin-glass-like overtraining phase. The mechanism is entropy–energy competition, shown on the continuous and Ising perceptrons: the Ising entropy vanishes near zero error, so the first-order condition loses its interior solution. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-542](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-542.md)); worth reading as the position paper that brought the statistical-mechanics theory of generalization back to deep learning: a network is idealized as a black box governed by a load-like parameter α (effective data per capacity, lowered by label noise) and a temperature-like parameter τ (raised by early stopping), and in the thermodynamic limit m, N → ∞ with α = m/N fixed, generalization has phases with sharp transitions. The mechanism is shown on the continuous versus Ising perceptron: where the entropy of near-optimal hypotheses vanishes (s(ε) ~ −(π²/2)ε² ln ε), the error drops discontinuously at αc, which PAC/VC bounds do not even qualitatively describe. A qualitative argument with no new theorem and no experiment. |
| [LIT-673](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-673.md) | Loss Surfaces, Mode Connectivity, and Fast Ensembling of DNNs | Garipov, Izmailov, Podoprikhin, Vetrov & Wilson (2018), NeurIPS 2018. Optima of deep networks trained from different initializations are joined by simple learned curves (a polygonal chain with one bend, or a quadratic Bezier curve) along which train loss and test error stay nearly constant, although the straight line between them rises to near-chance error. The curve is found by minimizing the loss averaged over a uniform t on the curve. Points along it are functionally diverse, which motivates Fast Geometric Ensembling: short cyclical learning-rate cycles late in training, collecting a checkpoint per cycle, beating Snapshot Ensembles on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet at equal budget. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-527](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-527.md)); one of the two founding demonstrations of mode connectivity. Two independently trained networks are joined by a learned one-bend polygonal chain or quadratic Bezier curve along which train loss and test error stay near the endpoints, while the straight segment between them climbs to near chance (VGG-16 on CIFAR-10: 90% test error at the midpoint). Points a short way along a curve already make useful ensemble partners, which motivates Fast Geometric Ensembling. The connectivity evidence is a table of single runs per architecture with no error bars, and the paper does not claim the curves are anything more than found. |
| [LIT-674](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-674.md) | Going Beyond Linear Mode Connectivity: The Layerwise Linear Feature Connectivity | Zhou, Yang, Yang, Yan & Hu (2023), NeurIPS 2023. When two trained networks are linearly mode connected, whether by spawning from a shared early checkpoint or by permutation alignment, the features of nearly every layer of the weight-interpolated network are proportional to the interpolation of the two networks' features (LLFC). LLFC on the output layer implies LMC. Weak additivity of ReLU and a commutativity condition between layers' weights and features together imply LLFC, and Git Re-Basin's two matching objectives are each one factor of the commutativity residual. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-512](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-512.md)); worth reading as the finding that linear mode connectivity reaches inside the network: whenever two trained networks are linearly connected, by spawning or by permutation, the feature map of almost every layer of the interpolated network points in the direction of the interpolated feature maps (LLFC). Two conditions, weak additivity of ReLU on the two networks' pre-activations and a commutativity of each layer's weights with the other network's features, imply exact LLFC (Theorem 1), and Git Re-Basin's weight and activation matching each minimise one factor of the commutativity residual. Image classification only. |
| [LIT-675](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-675.md) | TIES-Merging: Resolving Interference When Merging Models | Yadav, Tam, Choshen, Raffel & Bansal (2023), NeurIPS 2023. Merging fine-tuned models by averaging or adding task vectors suffers from two kinds of interference: redundant small updates dilute influential ones, and influential updates of different tasks disagree in sign. TIES-Merging trims each task vector to its top-k% magnitudes, elects a sign per parameter by total mass, and averages only values agreeing with it. It beats averaging, task arithmetic, Fisher merging and RegMean across (IA)³, T5 and ViT settings when a validation set tunes it, degrades more slowly as tasks are added, and with oracle signs nearly matches multitask training. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-526](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-526.md)); worth reading as the account of why averaging task vectors loses information: most of a fine-tuning update is small and redundant, and the influential coordinates of different tasks often disagree in sign, so a plain mean shrinks them. TIES-Merging keeps the top 20% of each task vector by magnitude, elects a sign per coordinate by total mass, and averages only the agreeing values. With a validation set it beats task arithmetic, Fisher merging and RegMean on all five settings (by 0.7 to 3.6 points); without one it falls below task arithmetic on T5-base (69.7 against 73.2 in Table 1), which the introduction's summary of results leaves out. With the multitask model's signs it reaches 72.0 against 73.1 for multitask training, which is the paper's strongest evidence that sign is the bottleneck. |
| [LIT-676](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-676.md) | Unveiling Mode Connectivity in Graph Neural Networks | Li, Chen, Han, Zeng, Liu & Tang (2025), preprint. GCN solutions for node classification from different seeds are connected by quadratic Bezier curves but often separated on the straight line, more so on co-authorship and heterophilous graphs than on citation graphs. GNN variants (GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT) give similar barriers, MLPs different ones. On CSBM graphs, barriers fall with density and feature separability and are highest at middling homophily. The authors bound the barrier through the spectral gap, bound the generalisation gap by the barrier, and propose a Wasserstein distance between graphs' interpolation-loss curves that correlates with transfer gaps. | Proposed — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-529](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-529.md)); watching, as the first study of mode connectivity in graph neural networks. Two GCNs trained on the same graph with different seeds are usually joined by a low-loss quadratic Bezier curve but often not by a straight line, and the barrier depends on the graph more than on the GNN variant: it falls with density, with feature separability, and with homophily far from one half, in synthetic CSBM graphs and, by the authors' reading, in 12 real ones. A loss-barrier bound, a generalisation bound in terms of the barrier, and a barrier-based distance between graphs are stated, but the appendix that should hold the proofs does not; the v1 text still carries an editor's placeholder. What would settle it: the proofs, and numbers for the barriers the figures show. |
| [LIT-677](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-677.md) | Unveiling mode-connectivity of the ELBO landscape | Zhang & Blei (2021), NeurIPS 2021 Bayesian Deep Learning workshop. Two SVI runs of LDA on the New York Times corpus give distinct local maxima of the ELBO; the simplified string method, with natural-gradient bead updates, is said to find an essentially flat maximum-energy path between them. Paths are said to flatten as data and the number of topics grow. The authors explain connectivity by over-parameterisation (more topics than the corpus holds) and by continuous statistical degeneracy, offering a landscape account of topic modelling's "no best answer". No results are reported in the paper. | Proposed — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-522](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-522.md)); watching, as the only work in the record to carry mode connectivity from neural networks to variational inference. It claims that local maxima of the LDA ELBO, from two SVI runs on the New York Times corpus, are joined by essentially flat maximum-energy paths found with the simplified string method, that paths flatten as the number of topics grows, and that statistical degeneracy explains this. The three-page workshop paper reports none of the results it describes: no path, no ELBO values, no synthetic-data experiment; its one figure is a schematic. What would settle it: the experiments themselves, which are not in this version. |
| [LIT-678](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-678.md) | Intermediate Layer Classifiers for OOD generalization | Uselis & Oh (2025), ICLR 2025. Linear probes on the frozen features of an intermediate layer (ILCs) are compared with last-layer retraining for out-of-distribution classification on CMNIST, Waterbirds, CelebA, MultiCelebA, CIFAR-10C, CIFAR-100C and ImageNet variants, with ResNets and ViTs. Few-shot (probe trained on OOD data), the best intermediate layer usually wins, by more when OOD data are scarce. Zero-shot (probe trained on ID data, OOD only for selecting the layer), it beats retraining the last layer, sharply under subpopulation shift. Layer L − 2 beats L − 1 in every dataset shown. A distance-ratio sensitivity score finds intermediate features less displaced by the shift than penultimate ones, most of all for minority groups. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-541](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-541.md)); worth reading as the measurement that, under distribution shift, a trained classifier's best linear probe is usually not on the penultimate layer: Intermediate Layer Classifiers (linear probes on frozen layer-l features, l ≤ L − 2) beat last-layer retraining in the few-shot setting on most of nine shifted datasets, and, trained only on in-distribution data, raise worst-group accuracy from 79.4% to 87.1% on Waterbirds and 56.0% to 82.0% on CelebA. The proposed reason is that penultimate features move further under shift, especially for minority groups, while intermediate ones stay put. Selection of the layer uses OOD validation data, and the gains for ViTs are small. |
| [LIT-679](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-679.md) | A Random Matrix Analysis of Random Fourier Features: Beyond the Gaussian Kernel, a Precise Phase Transition, and the Corresponding Double Descent | Liao, Couillet & Mahoney (2020), NeurIPS 2020 and J. Stat. Mech. (2021). For random Fourier features ΣX = [cos(WX); sin(WX)] with n, p, N large and comparable, the expected resolvent of ΣXᵀΣX/n is asymptotically Q̄ = ((N/n)(Kcos/(1+δcos) + Ksin/(1+δsin)) + λI)⁻¹, with δσ = (1/n)tr KσQ̄, not the Gaussian-kernel prediction. Closed forms for training and test MSE follow and match MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and Kannada-MNIST. In the ridgeless limit the δ jump at 2N = n, separating an under- and an over-parameterized phase; the test MSE diverges there unless test data sit within about λ of the training data, which is the double-descent peak. A tuned λ removes it. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-519](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-519.md)); worth reading as an exact random-matrix account of double descent in random Fourier feature ridge regression when n, p and N are large together: the RFF Gram matrix does not converge to the Gaussian kernel in spectral norm, but its resolvent has a deterministic equivalent built from the cos and sin kernels with corrections δcos, δsin solving a fixed point (Theorem 1). Training and test MSE follow in closed form (Theorems 2–3). As λ → 0 the δ jump from O(1) to order 1/λ across 2N = n, so the model has two phases, and the test error diverges at the boundary when test data differ from training data; that singularity is the double-descent peak. Data need only be concentrated random vectors, not Gaussian. |
| [LIT-680](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-680.md) | Proving Linear Mode Connectivity of Neural Networks via Optimal Transport | Ferbach, Goujaud, Gidel & Dieuleveut (2024), AISTATS 2024. Finding the permutation that aligns two networks' neurons layer by layer is an optimal-transport problem between empirical weight distributions, so Wasserstein convergence rates bound when the permuted straight line stays low-loss. Wide two-layer nets trained by SGD in the mean-field regime are linearly connected modulo permutation with high probability. Deep nets with i.i.d. neuron weights (as at initialization) are too, once each layer is wider than about (1/ε) to the power of the previous one, a rate shown tight. Low-dimensional weight distributions need less width, and a covariance-weighted weight matching beats plain weight matching. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-543](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-543.md)); the first proof of linear mode connectivity modulo permutation beyond a single hidden layer. Aligning neurons is an optimal-transport problem between the empirical distributions of their weights, so convergence rates of empirical measures in Wasserstein distance bound how wide a network must be for the permuted straight line to stay low-loss. It proves the result for wide two-layer nets trained by SGD in the mean-field regime, and for deep nets whenever neuron weights within a layer are i.i.d., which holds at initialization. The width needed grows like (1/ε) to the power of the previous layer's width, a rate shown to be tight, and falls if weights concentrate near a low-dimensional subspace. The proofs rest on independence of neurons, which the authors call the central and least realistic assumption. |
| [LIT-681](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-681.md) | Optimizing Mode Connectivity for Class Incremental Learning | Wen, Cheng, Qiu, Wang, Pan & Li (2023), ICML 2023. In class-incremental learning the linear path between adjacent continual minima crosses a high-loss ridge for earlier tasks. OPC finds a curved low-loss path, modelled as the line plus a layer-wise Fourier-series perturbation, with the path loss split at a switching point between old-task and new-task memory losses. EOPC averages points in a cylinder around the switching point and is added as post-processing to existing methods, improving PODNet and AANet on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100 and ImageNet-1K and sharply reducing forgetting. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-524](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-524.md)); worth reading as the class-incremental counterpart of Mirzadeh et al.: between adjacent continual minima in class-incremental learning, the straight line crosses a high-loss ridge for the earlier tasks, and a curved path avoids it. OPC parameterises that path as the line plus a layer-wise Fourier perturbation that vanishes at both ends (2 × 96 × 4 learned numbers for a 96-layer ResNet), splits the path loss at a switching point into old-task and new-task halves, and pushes it to flat regions by sampling a cylinder around it. Averaging points near the switching point (EOPC) adds 0.3 to 5.1 points of average incremental accuracy to PODNet and AANet on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100 and ImageNet-1K. In Table 4 it beats Bezier and simplex paths only on the longer task sequences. |
| [LIT-682](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-682.md) | Exploring Neural Network Landscapes: Star-Shaped and Geodesic Connectivity | Lin, Li & Wu (2024), preprint. For a two-layer ReLU student of an orthonormal teacher, and for deep linear networks, over-parameterisation makes any two global minima two-piece linearly connected and gives any finite set of minima a common centre linearly connected to each (star- shaped connectivity). Under a sparsity bias like SGD's, the shortest path on the minimum manifold is nearly as short as the straight line, with normalised geodesic distance ≤ 1 + c₂/(r√m). A centre-finding objective locates such centres for independently trained FNNs, VGG16 and ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-10, with no permutation alignment. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-535](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-535.md)); worth reading as the theory of star-shaped connectivity without permutations. For a two-layer ReLU student of an orthonormal teacher, and for deep linear networks, sufficiently wide networks have any two minima joined by a two-piece linear path and any finite set of minima linearly joined to a common centre on the minimum manifold. SGD's bias toward sparse solutions explains why the shortest path on the manifold is nearly as short as the straight line (normalised geodesic distance ≤ 1 + c₂/(r√m)). Experiments find centres for three to five independently trained FNNs, VGG16s and ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-10 with almost no barrier. Preprint. |
| [LIT-683](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-683.md) | Exact expressions for double descent and implicit regularization via surrogate random design | Dereziński, Liang & Mahoney (2019), NeurIPS 2020. For the Moore–Penrose estimator X⁺y in linear regression, a determinantal surrogate design (density ∝ pdet(XXᵀ), Poisson sample size with mean n) gives exact MSE: σ² tr((Σ + λnI)⁻¹)(1 − αn)/(d − n) + w*ᵀ(Σ + λnI)⁻¹w*·(d − n)/tr((Σ + λnI)⁻¹) for n < d, σ² tr(Σ⁻¹) at n = d, σ² tr(Σ⁻¹)(1 − βn)/(n − d) for n > d, where n = tr(Σ(Σ + λnI)⁻¹).
