| [LIT-970](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-970.md) v2 | Symmetry in Neural Network Parameter Spaces | Zhao, Walters & Yu (2025), TMLR. A survey of parameter-space symmetries: transformations of a network's parameters that leave its function, or its loss, unchanged. It catalogues them for common components (linear layers, homogeneous and other activations, normalization, softmax, attention, LoRA). It surveys when they are complete, so that parameters are identifiable up to them. Continuous symmetries stretch minima into connected manifolds and discrete ones replicate them. Under gradient flow, continuous symmetries give conserved quantities, such as layer imbalance, that label trajectories and locate the endpoint among the minima. Finite steps, gradient noise and weight decay break these conservation laws. | Active — read 2026-10-13 ([NOTE-712](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-712.md)): §§1–5 and 7–8 in full, §6 in part. A survey, so its claims about the works it cites are secondhand here. It bears on [QUESTION-058](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-058.md) and [QUESTION-069](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-069.md), and on the null space that [THEORY-209](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-209.md) leaves out. The account filed from it is [THEORY-210](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-210.md). |
| [LIT-971](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-971.md) v2 | Is Model Collapse Inevitable? Breaking the Curse of Recursion by Accumulating Real and Synthetic Data | Gerstgrasser et al. (2024). Small language models (9M–126M) and a molecular diffusion model trained for five to eight rounds on their predecessors' samples degrade when each round's data replace the last, and hold their test loss when the samples accumulate alongside the real data; a VAE's error still rises under accumulation, more slowly. In a fixed-design linear regression it proves that accumulation gives test error σ²d/(T−d−1)·Σ1/i², bounded by π²/6 times the first round's, where replacement gives σ²d/(T−d−1)·n. The error is bounded, not constant. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-815](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-815.md)) in full; worth reading for [QUESTION-016](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-016.md) as an exact, bounded case of degradation along a reconstruction chain: in a fixed-design linear regression refit to its own labels, keeping all earlier data gives test error σ²d/(T−d−1)·Σ1/i², below π²/6 times the first fit's, where replacing the data gives linear growth. Read it knowing that the error still rises every round, that what is retained is the source sample in the training pool, not an interpreter's side information, and that one squared-error task is measured, not sufficiency. Filed as [THEORY-289](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-289.md). |

For 24 factual relations, how well an affine map from subject to object representation reproduces the model (linear relational embedding causality) correlates with the relation's mean subject–object co-occurrence count in pretraining (r = 0.82), more than with subject (0.66) or object (0.59) frequency alone. Mean causality passes 0.9 above about 1.1k co-occurrences in GPT-J, 2.0k in OLMo-7B and 4.4k in OLMo-1B, at whatever training step the count is reached. A regression on LRE quality predicts a term's pretraining frequency within 10× more often than log probabilities do, also for a second model. Correlational, by the authors' own statement. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-786](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-786.md)) in full; worth reading as the clearest measurement of when linear structure forms in trained language models: across 24 factual relations in OLMo-1B, OLMo-7B and GPT-J, the quality of a linear relational embedding tracks mean subject–object co-occurrence in pretraining (r = 0.82), with mean causality above 0.9 past about 4.4k, 2.0k and 1.1k co-occurrences, at any training step. Read it knowing that it is correlational by the authors' own statement, that an LRE is an affine map between hidden states for one relation and not an attribute direction, and that the structure of co-occurrence across attributes is not measured. | [LIT-974](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-974.md) v2 | Neural Collapse Under MSE Loss: Proximity to and Dynamics on the Central Path | Han, Papyan & Donoho (2021; ICLR 2022). Networks trained with MSE loss show neural collapse, on five datasets with VGG, ResNet and DenseNet. The MSE loss splits exactly into a term where the classifier is the least-squares classifier for the current features and a non-negative deviation term. The deviation is measured to be negligible from early in training: the "central path". On that path, for unconstrained features with no weight decay and re-whitened to identity within-class covariance after every step, gradient flow gives closed-form dynamics. Every singular value of Σ_W^(−1/2)M̃ grows as (4t/N)^(1/4), and they tend to equality, which yields NC1–NC4. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-783](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-783.md)) in full; worth reading as the record's one derivation of neural-collapse dynamics in closed form. Under MSE loss, a trained classifier stays near the least-squares classifier for its own features (measured), and on that central path a whitened gradient flow of unconstrained features drives every class-separation singular value to infinity as (4t/N)^(1/4) and to equality, which is NC1 and NC2. It also measures collapse under MSE on five datasets and three architectures. Read it knowing that the flow is not gradient descent (features are re-whitened after every step), that the theory has no weight decay while every experiment has it, that it is MSE and not cross-entropy, and that the experiments are [LIT-618](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-618.md)'s protocol with one run per cell. |

In small CIFAR and MNIST autoencoders whose affine maps, initialisation and optimiser are all rotation-equivariant, only the activation is changed. Elementwise tanh (signed-permutation symmetry) and Leaky-ReLU (permutation symmetry) concentrate latent representations into near-discrete beams along the basis or the ±1 diagonal, even before any activation. Radial versions of the same functions, equivariant to the orthogonal group, leave them continuous. A new projection method (PPP) shows this in density plots; there is no statistic. The paper argues that the primitives' algebraic symmetry predicts task-agnostic representational structure. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-759](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-759.md)) in full; worth reading as a clean ablation in which the activation function is the only part of an autoencoder that singles out a basis: elementwise tanh (B_n) and Leaky-ReLU (S_n) drive latent representations into narrow beams arranged by their group, even in layers no activation precedes, while radial O(n)-equivariant versions leave them spread. Read it knowing that the evidence is density plots from small CIFAR and MNIST autoencoders, five seeds a condition, with no statistic, and that its claims about grandmother neurons, superposition, neural collapse and better reconstruction are conjecture or preliminary. The paper argues that analogy parallelograms are in the co-occurrence data, not made by word2vec. On Wikipedia, an SVD of log raw co-occurrence counts solves 61% of the Google analogies over a 1,487-word vocabulary (50% over 10,072), and word2vec without negative sampling about 60%, against 75% for word2vec trained on the full corpus. Raw rows solve under 6%. That is a data-side account in which aspects combine as a mixture, so raw counts and not PMI are linear. Read it knowing that the theorem covers one 24-sentence design and exact shapes, that its aspects are independent (a Boolean lattice), that the real-text analogy results need log counts and an SVD, and that the restricted word2vec baseline is trained on a dummy corpus. | [LIT-978](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-978.md) v3 | Neural Collapse: A Review on Modelling Principles and Generalization | Kothapalli (2022; TMLR 2023). A survey of neural collapse in one notation. It reviews the unconstrained-features model and local elasticity as ways of modelling how training reaches the collapsed state. Every derivation it covers works with features cut loose from the data. On generalization it finds the literature in conflict: collapse on the training set does not fix test error, and collapse on test data is weaker and depends on the dataset. No agreed threshold says when a network is collapsed. It reports Kornblith et al.'s finding that more collapsed ImageNet networks transfer worse. Skimmed. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-772](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-772.md)) in part; worth reading as the map of the first two years of models of neural collapse, sorted into unconstrained-features models and local elasticity, with their assumptions side by side, and as the place where the conflicting claims about collapse and generalization are set next to each other: collapse on the training set reached by different optimizers with different test error, weaker and dataset-dependent collapse on test data, and worse transfer from more collapsed ImageNet networks. Skimmed: the equations were not checked. |
| [LIT-981](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-981.md) v2 | Geometric diffusions as a tool for harmonic analysis and structure definition of data: Diffusion maps | Coifman et al. (2005). A symmetric, positivity-preserving, positive semi-definite affinity kernel is normalized into a Markov operator that is conjugate to a symmetric one. Its leading eigenfunctions, scaled by powers of their eigenvalues, embed the data so that Euclidean distance equals diffusion distance at each scale. A one-parameter normalization yields the graph Laplacian, the backward Fokker–Planck operator, or the Laplace–Beltrami operator, the last independent of sampling density. The convergence theorem is stated without proof. Non-symmetric kernels are not treated. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-784](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-784.md)) in part; worth reading for [QUESTION-052](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-052.md) as the classical symmetric case. From a symmetric, positive semi-definite affinity, a Markov operator conjugate to a symmetric one yields eigenfunction coordinates in which Euclidean distance is diffusion distance. A density-corrected normalization recovers the Laplace–Beltrami operator independent of sampling. Read it knowing that the PMC copy's equations could not be seen here, that its one theorem is stated without proof, and that its "directed diffusion" is anisotropic, not a non-reversible chain. |

The paper writes NC1, as tr Σ_W / tr Σ_B, for the features of any kernel. It proves, for one-dimensional two-class Gaussian data on opposite sides of the origin with ReLU and zero bias, that the NTK of a wide two-layer net has the same expected NC1 as the NNGP kernel at initialization. In higher dimensions it measures the NTK no more collapsed, and with ReLU less. A data-aware adaptive kernel lowers NC1 and approximates finite networks on separable data. It departs from them under class overlap in high dimension and under imbalance. Erf activation gives lower NC1 than ReLU. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-774](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-774.md)) in full; worth reading as the record's one account of neural collapse in which the data enter, and for its negative result. In the case it can solve, lazy-regime training of a wide two-layer net leaves the within-class variability of the features exactly where initialization put it, because there the NTK is a within-class rescaling of the NNGP kernel. It also gives NC1 as a closed function of any kernel matrix. Read it knowing that the theorem covers one-dimensional data with two classes on opposite sides of the origin and zero bias, that the higher-dimensional claim is simulation (and for ReLU the NTK is less collapsed, not equal), that its NC1 is tr Σ_W / tr Σ_B on shallow MSE-trained binary nets, and that the data-aware kernel it proposes fails under class overlap and imbalance. Its printed Eq. 16 appears to keep a cross-class term the kernel sets to zero. |
| [LIT-986](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-986.md) v2 | Transformers learn factored representations | Shai et al. (2026). If a sequence generator's latent operators are tensor products, its predictive state stays a product of per-factor beliefs. A linear map embeds that state losslessly in orthogonal subspaces of total dimension Σ(d_n − 1), against (Π d_n) − 1 for the joint state. Small transformers trained on five such synthetic factors settle near 10 dimensions against 242, in approximately orthogonal subspaces. When token noise makes factoring lossy they collapse to the factored form first and expand later, the more so the more noise. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-758](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-758.md)) in full; worth reading for [QUESTION-060](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-060.md) as a controlled case with known relevant variables. | [LIT-994](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-994.md) v2 | Imbalance Trouble: Revisiting Neural-Collapse Geometry | Thrampoulidis, Kini, Vakilian & Behnia (2022, NeurIPS). In the unconstrained-features model under STEP class imbalance, every solution of the max-margin problem, the limit of cross-entropy with vanishing regularization, has logits equal to the simplex-encoded label matrix Ẑ. Its classifier and embedding Gram matrices come from Ẑ's SVD (SELI). That is the simplex ETF only for balanced or binary data. With any finite ridge the geometry differs and depends on its strength; it tends to SELI as the ridge vanishes. The classifier and embedding geometries come from that matrix's SVD, and they are the simplex ETF only for balanced or binary data. Majority classifiers come out longer and minority classifiers closer together, and the minority-collapse threshold is given in closed form. Read it knowing that gradient descent is only conjectured to reach this geometry, that under any finite weight decay the geometry differs and depends on its strength, that convergence is slow and slower with imbalance, and that the deep-net runs are one seed per cell with weight decay on. |

| [LIT-1012](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1012.md) | Noise Balance and Stationary Distribution of Stochastic Gradient Descent | Ziyin, Li & Ueda (2023; v2 2025). Under the SDE model of SGD with temperature T = η/S, a rescaling symmetry between parameter groups u and w gives d(‖u‖² − ‖w‖²)/dt = −T(uᵀC₁u − wᵀC₂w): the Brownian term vanishes, and minibatch noise drives the quantity to the point where the two groups' gradient noise balances. A differentiable symmetry of the loss makes the gradient orthogonal to the symmetry's generator and constrains the Hessian. Under gradient flow each symmetry then conserves a quantity: translation (softmax) the parameter sum, scale (batchnorm) the norm, and rescale (homogeneous activations) the difference of squared norms. A loss has an O-mirror symmetry if it is invariant under the reflection I − 2OOᵀ. Rescaling, rotation and permutation symmetries all imply mirror symmetries. | [LIT-1044](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1044.md) v2 | Why Do Better Loss Functions Lead to Less Transferable Features? | Kornblith, Chen, Lee & Norouzi (2020; NeurIPS 2021). Nine training objectives for ResNet-50 on ImageNet: seven beat softmax cross-entropy significantly, by up to 0.9 points top-1, and all eight alternatives yield fixed penultimate features that transfer worse to eight new-class datasets, by linear and k-NN readout. Each raises penultimate-layer class separation R² (one minus within-class over total cosine distance), and mean linear transfer falls with R² across losses (Spearman ρ = −0.93) and along a cosine-softmax temperature sweep. The losses differ only in the last third of the network, and full fine-tuning removes the gap. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-762](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-762.md)) in full; worth reading as the record's one direct measurement of what class separation in the last layers costs off the trained task. Across nine objectives for ResNet-50 on ImageNet, those that beat softmax cross-entropy all raise penultimate-layer class separation (R² 0.349 → up to 0.845), and mean linear transfer to eight new-class datasets falls with it (Spearman ρ = −0.93; 75.9% for softmax, 48.3% for squared error). Cosine-softmax temperature moves both on one knob. The losses differ only in the last third of the network, and full fine-tuning erases the transfer gap. Read it knowing that the networks are early-stopped at 91.6–93.6% training accuracy, so this is relative within-class variance and not terminal-phase neural collapse; that the cost is for new classes, while on shifted ImageNet test sets with the same classes the more separated losses do slightly better (Table C.2); and that it is one dataset, two architectures and a correlation across losses, with one within-loss sweep. Filed as [THEORY-246](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-246.md). |
| [LIT-1052](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1052.md) | Calibration for the (Computationally-Identifiable) Masses | Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold and Rothblum (2018), ICML; arXiv 1711.08513. A predictor is α-multicalibrated on a collection C of subpopulations if, within every set S in C, the individuals given (roughly) the same prediction v have true probabilities averaging within α of v, except on an α-fraction of S. For any C whose sets have size at least γN, a simple iterative patching algorithm reaches multicalibration from O(log\|C\|/α^{11/2}γ^{3/2}) samples in time linear in \|C\|, and the result is a circuit only O(s/α⁴γ) in size when the sets of C are computed by size-s circuits. Learning it is equivalent, up to polynomial factors, to weak agnostic learning of C, so it is hard for rich C under cryptographic assumptions. Calibrating any predictor h on its own level sets as well as on C costs at most 6α in squared error. All guarantees are relative to the benchmark p*, which is itself defined relative to the features available, and they hold only for large sets; the paper offers no uniqueness for the predictor and does not state a theorem in indistinguishability form. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' arXiv preprint, latest version v2 of 16 March 2018 (arxiv.org/pdf/1711.08513, 40 pp.); the ICML version (PMLR 80:1939–1948, proceedings.mlr.press/v80/hebert-johnson18a/hebert-johnson18a.pdf, with a supplement) was fetched and its definitions and theorem statements compared, not read in full. Worth reading as the source definition of multicalibration: calibration required on every set in a collection C of large, efficiently identifiable subpopulations; a patching algorithm that reaches it from O(log\|C\|/α^{11/2}γ^{3/2}) samples in time linear in \|C\|, with a circuit of size O(s/α⁴γ); learning it equivalent to weak agnostic learning of C, and so hard for rich C under cryptographic assumptions; and calibration on any predictor's level sets at almost no cost in squared error. Its multi-AE (accuracy in expectation on every S in C) is what later work calls multiaccuracy; the paper does not use that word. For [QUESTION-103](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-103.md) it supplies adequacy relative to a class of observers in correlation form (a violation is a set in C correlating with the residual), but it states no indistinguishability theorem, no distinguishing advantage and nothing from signal detection; that framing is Dwork et al.'s ([LIT-1068](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1068.md)). For [CLAIM-152](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-152.md) it is consistent and adds a second relativity: adequacy is relative to the outcome, to the features through p*, and to the class C, and even with all three fixed the adequate predictor is not unique. For [QUESTION-104](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-104.md) it gives a formal instance of budget-relative sufficiency in which representing an adequate predictor is cheap (only modestly larger than the observer class) while finding one can be hard, but it has no notion of an optimal partition and does not show one changing with the budget. |
| [LIT-1063](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1063.md) | Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters | Snell, Lee, Xu and Kumar (2024, arXiv 2408.03314; ICLR 2025). On MATH with PaLM 2-S*, which way of spending test-time compute works best (beam search against a process reward model versus best-of-N; sequential self-revision versus parallel sampling) depends on how hard the question is for the base model, and choosing the method per difficulty bin matches best-of-N with up to about 4× less test-time compute (the discussion says 2–4×). In a FLOPs-matched comparison with a ~14× larger model, the extra test-time compute a small model may spend is set by R, the ratio of total inference tokens to pretraining tokens: when R is small the larger model's pretraining cost buys many samples per query and test-time compute wins on easy and medium questions; when R is large the budget per query falls toward the parameter ratio and the larger model wins, always on the hardest questions. Difficulty estimation (2048 samples per question) and verifier and revision-model finetuning are not counted in the compute, R is an aggregate token ratio with no term for which queries recur, and the evidence is one model family on one benchmark of 500 test questions. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the arXiv preprint (arxiv.org/pdf/2408.03314, v1 of 2024-08-06, the only arXiv version) and from the ICLR 2025 conference version, open access in the ICLR proceedings (proceedings.iclr.cc, retitled "... than Scaling Parameters for Reasoning"), which is a revision not posted to arXiv: it charges verifier calls to inference FLOPs, which halves the stated R values (0.16/0.79/22 become 0.08/0.40/11) at unchanged budgets, and adds a verifier-quality check. Worth reading as the standard empirical case that the best use of inference compute depends on how hard a question is for the base model, and that choosing the method per difficulty bin matches best-of-N with up to about 4× less test-time compute on MATH with PaLM 2-S*, before counting the 2048-sample difficulty estimate. For [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it shows a FLOPs-matched amortization model: a ~14× larger model's extra pretraining is a fixed cost spread over all inference, so the per-query test-time budget it buys scales as M + 3(M − 1)/R, with R the ratio of inference to pretraining tokens; test-time compute wins at low R on easy and medium questions and loses at high R and on the hardest questions at every R. R is aggregate inference volume, not a count of recurring queries; the larger model's per-token cost is a retrieval-cost term; query predictability appears as difficulty but its cost is not counted; staleness and erosion are absent. |
| [LIT-1068](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1068.md) | Outcome Indistinguishability | Dwork, Kim, Reingold, Rothblum and Yona (2021), STOC; arXiv 2011.13426. A predictor p̃ is outcome indistinguishable (OI) relative to a class A of distinguishers when no A ∈ A can tell an individual with Nature's outcome from the same individual with an outcome drawn from Ber(p̃_i). The paper sets out four levels by how much access the distinguisher has to p̃: none, the prediction on the sampled individual, oracle queries, or the code. The lower two levels are equivalent to multi-accuracy and multi-calibration over closely related classes. At those levels OI predictors exist with size O(s/ε²), whatever Nature's complexity. At the oracle level, under fine-grained hardness of clique counting or BPP ≠ PSPACE, some efficient distinguisher classes force any OI predictor to be nearly as expensive as Nature's own predictor. That gives a strict separation between oracle access and sample access. OI never requires p̃ ≈ p*. A predictor is good only relative to A, and with the paper's construction a weak A gives a coarse predictor that a richer A would refute. The paper covers binary outcomes, a fixed representation of individuals and single samples (multi-sample OI is left mostly to future work). | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the arXiv preprint, arXiv:2011.13426v1 (arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13426, 61 pp.), the only arXiv version. The STOC 2021 version of record (doi:10.1145/3406325.3451064) was not read; its only open copies are submitted versions (arXiv, MIT DSpace). The recurrence algebra of Theorems 5.9–5.10 and the proof of Proposition 6.3 were checked for structure only. Worth reading as the source of outcome indistinguishability. A predictor is adequate relative to a class A of distinguishers when none can tell its sampled outcomes from Nature's. The paper sets out four levels by the distinguisher's access to the predictor (none, the sampled prediction, oracle queries, the code). It proves the lower two equivalent to multi-accuracy and multi-calibration and gives OI predictors of size O(s/ε²) whatever Nature's complexity. At the oracle level it gives conditional hardness (clique counting, or BPP ≠ PSPACE): cheap distinguishers with query access can force any OI predictor to be about as costly as Nature's own. For [QUESTION-103](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-103.md) it supplies the formal half: distinguishing advantage is the ROC quantity, and with all subset distinguishers it becomes statistical distance. It says nothing about SDT, criteria or ideal-observer efficiency, and adds that access as well as budget sets an observer's power. For [CLAIM-152](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-152.md) it is an instance of adequacy relative to the observer class with the target held fixed, with no uniqueness or minimality of the predictor. For [QUESTION-104](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-104.md) it shows a restricted class accepting a coarser model (p̃ ≡ 1/2 where Nature's two halves are computationally indistinguishable), but at the oracle and code levels a bounded observer need not be satisfied by a cheap model. |
| [LIT-1069](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1069.md) | Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games | Jones (2021), arXiv 2104.03113. Training AlphaZero on Hex at board sizes 3×3 to 9×9, the best Elo reachable for a given training compute follows one change-point curve across sizes: an incline of about 500 Elo per tenfold of training compute, with the compute for perfect play rising about 7× and the compute to leave random play about 4× per added board row, and fits on small boards predicting larger ones. On 9×9 only, train-time and test-time (tree-search) compute substitute at a fixed rate: at equal Elo, each 10× of train-time compute removes about 15× of test-time compute (fit: log test = −1.2·log train + 0.004·Elo + 29), down to a one-node search, over roughly 1e14–1e16 FLOPS-seconds of training. The trade is an iso-performance curve for a single search; the paper never counts how many games or moves the trained agent will play, so it does not price amortization, and it does not state the unit of test-time compute. One game, small boards, Elo anchored to a perfect player, and no uncertainty on the fitted trade-off coefficients. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the author's arXiv preprint, version 2 of 2021-04-15, the latest (arxiv.org/pdf/2104.03113v2; v1 diffed against it, same methods and numbers). Worth reading as a clean small-scale scaling law in problem size as well as compute: AlphaZero on Hex, boards 3×3 to 9×9, one change-point frontier of about 500 Elo per tenfold of training compute, with the compute for perfect play rising about 7× per added board row and fits on small boards predicting larger ones. For [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it shows that, on 9×9 at fixed Elo, training and tree-search compute substitute along a straight log–log line, about 15× less search per 10× more training (fit: log test = −1.2·log train + 0.004·Elo + 29), over roughly 1e14–1e16 FLOPS-seconds of training and down to a one-node search; it does not count the games or moves the trained agent will play, or define the unit of test-time compute, so it prices the iso-performance substitution but not amortization, and has no terms for query shift, staleness or erosion of search. |
| [LIT-1070](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1070.md) | Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws | Sardana, Portes, Doubov and Frankle (2024, ICML; arXiv 2401.00448). Fixing a target pre-training loss and adding inference FLOPs (2N per token over a known lifetime demand D_inf) to training FLOPs (6N per token), the compute-minimising model is smaller and trained on more data than Chinchilla-optimal, increasingly so as D_inf approaches and exceeds the training-set size; the optimum has no closed form and is found numerically. The savings are modest in FLOPs (for a 30B-Chinchilla-quality model with 10^13 inference tokens, 28% by training 13.6B on 2.84× the data) and larger in dollars once inference's low hardware utilisation is priced in (17% to 58% in the paper's examples). 47 training runs (150M–6B parameters, 10–10,000 tokens per parameter) find loss still falling at extreme ratios, but more slowly than Chinchilla-fitted laws predict, so the formula overstates the gain from long training. Demand is assumed known before training and fixed given quality; there is no term for uncertainty, discounting, obsolescence or a model being replaced. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' arXiv preprint v3 (arxiv.org/pdf/2401.00448v3, 14 Apr 2025), which is the ICML 2024 paper (PMLR 235, also fetched from proceedings.mlr.press/v235/sardana24a.html and diffed: same equations, tables and numbers, small wording edits); v1 (2023-12-31) is an earlier two-author NeurIPS 2023 workshop version without the experiments. Worth reading as the worked case of choosing how much to precompute by expected use: fixing quality, it adds lifetime inference FLOPs (2N per token) to training FLOPs (6N per token), finds the optimum numerically (no closed form), and shows the optimal model shrinking and training longer as demand grows (30B-Chinchilla quality with 10^13 inference tokens: 13.6B on 2.84× the data, 28% fewer FLOPs; in dollars, with inference at 1% utilisation, savings of 17% to 58%), with 47 training runs up to 10,000 tokens per parameter showing quality still improving but more slowly than the fitted law predicts. For [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it supplies expected reuse and a non-zero per-use cost as explicit terms, and nothing for staleness, uncertainty about demand (assumed known before training) or erosion; for [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it instantiates the break-even n > F/(c_r − c_a − u) with u = 0, and shows the choice as a continuous dial tied by a production function rather than a file-or-not decision. |
| [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md) | Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), IEEE TPAMI 2020. HNSW is a stack of proximity graphs on nested random subsets of the data. Each element's top layer is drawn from a geometric distribution, and new neighbours are chosen by a pruning rule that favours diverse directions. Searching from the sparse top layer down makes per-query cost grow about logarithmically with N on uniform random data in 4 and 8 dimensions, which flat NSW graphs did not. The logarithmic bound is derived only for exact Delaunay graphs of bounded mean degree, which HNSW does not build. For the graphs it does build, logarithmic scaling is measured, at low dimension only, and on 200M SIFT vectors the paper reports the scaling "deviates from the pure logarithm". The neighbour-selection rule is what keeps clustered data searchable: in the paper's synthetic test with 100 isolated clusters, linking each element to its nearest neighbours fails to reach high recall. There is no worst-case or recall guarantee, no deletion, and no analysis of query distributions unlike the data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' arXiv preprint, version 4 of 14 August 2018 (arxiv.org/pdf/1603.09320v4, 13 pp., the last arXiv version, whose abstract matches the published one apart from copy-editing; the TPAMI body was not seen). Version 1 (2016) was compared: it claimed deletion, which v4 drops and lists as future work. Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open-access copy of the TPAMI version. Worth reading as the source of the hierarchical graph index: nested proximity graphs on geometrically sampled layers, with a neighbour rule that keeps links between clusters. Its logarithmic search cost is derived only for exact Delaunay graphs of bounded degree, which it does not build, and is measured only on uniform random data in 4 and 8 dimensions; on 200M SIFT the scaling "deviates from the pure logarithm". It gives no worst-case or recall guarantee and no deletion. For [CLAIM-310](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-310.md) it shows, with bins replaced by graphs, that the arrangement of fixed data under a fixed distance decides cost and, on clustered data, whether items can be found at all; it narrows part 2, since the index is built without any query mix and every test drew its queries from the data. | [LIT-1112](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1112.md) | Worst-case Performance of Popular Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Implementations: Guarantees and Limitations | Indyk and Xu (2023), NeurIPS 2023. For DiskANN's "slow preprocessing" graph (each point linked to the points that survive α-pruning of all other points, naively O(n³) time), greedy search from any start with no backtracking reaches a ((α+1)/(α−1) + ε)-approximate nearest neighbour in O(log_α(∆/((α−1)ε))) steps, each costing O((4α)^d log ∆) for doubling dimension d and aspect ratio ∆; the ratio is tight and the dependence on ∆ cannot be replaced by log n. For DiskANN with its practical "fast preprocessing", HNSW, NSG and seven other graph indexes, the paper constructs two-dimensional point sets (constant doubling dimension) on which, in experiments with the authors' code at the authors' recommended parameters, the search queue must hold about 10% of the points before recall@5 becomes non-zero or the approximation ratio becomes reasonable. The linear lower bounds are empirical, for one query per constructed instance, with an informal Ω(n/R) argument for fast-preprocessing DiskANN; no theorem bounds HNSW or NSG. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 (NOTE for LIT-1112) from the authors' arXiv preprint (arxiv.org/abs/2310.19126v1, the only version, which carries the NeurIPS 2023 line and is the camera-ready text), including Appendices A–C. Worth reading as the first worst-case analysis of graph-based nearest neighbour indexes: DiskANN built by "slow preprocessing" (every point pruned against all others with α > 1, naively O(n³)) is proved to give a ((α+1)/(α−1) + ε)-approximate neighbour in O(log_α(∆/((α−1)ε))) greedy steps of cost O((4α)^d log ∆), for doubling dimension d and aspect ratio ∆, with both the ratio and the ∆ dependence shown tight; for DiskANN as implemented, HNSW, NSG and seven others, two-dimensional constructed instances made recall@5 zero or near zero until the search queue held about 10% of the points, an empirical result with no theorem behind it for those algorithms. For [CLAIM-310](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-310.md), with [LIT-1103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1103.md), it shows on one fixed point set that the graph built over it, not the points, decides between finding the nearest neighbour in two steps and scanning a tenth of the collection, and that the guarantee rests on a stated property of the arrangement (from every point, some edge gets α times closer to any target); for [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it is a case where an expensive build buys a worst-case guarantee, without a measured break-even or upkeep. |

| [LIT-1246](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1246.md) v3 | Diffusion maps | Coifman & Lafon (2006). From a symmetric non-negative kernel, a reversible random walk; its t-step diffusion distance equals the Euclidean distance between eigenvectors weighted by λ_l^t, and truncating where \|λ_l\|^t ≤ δ\|λ₁\|^t gives the diffusion map, whose dimension falls as t grows. An α-normalization by a kernel density estimate gives, as the kernel width ε → 0, a generator with invariant density q^{2(1−α)}: the density-weighted graph Laplacian at α = 0, the Fokker–Planck (Langevin) operator at α = 1/2, and the Laplace–Beltrami operator, free of the density, at α = 1. Symmetric kernels only. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-985](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-985.md)) in full; worth reading for [QUESTION-217](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-217.md) as the model case of a coarse-to-fine order induced by an operator rather than an imposed partition, and for the proofs the PNAS announcement ([LIT-981](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-981.md)) deferred. The diffusion distance D_t is exactly the Euclidean distance between eigenvector coordinates weighted by λ_l^t. The number of steps t is a scale, and the kernel width ε is a second one. An α-normalization makes the small-ε limit the graph Laplacian with a density term (α = 0), the Langevin generator whose invariant density is the sampling density (α = 1/2), or the Laplace–Beltrami operator (α = 1). Read it knowing that Proposition 1's "relative accuracy δ" for the truncated map is wrong (the bound is absolute, [THEORY-745](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-745.md)); that Appendix A's ψ_l = φ_l/π should be φ_l/√π; that the α = 1/2 display, the circle formula, the discrete kernel of §5 and Criterion 4's exponent are misprinted or wrong; that the boundary rate and the heat-kernel proof are incomplete ([THEORY-744](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-744.md)); and that no spectral gap is used anywhere. |
| [LIT-1249](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1249.md) v3 | Slow Feature Analysis: Unsupervised Learning of Invariances | Wiskott & Sejnowski (2002). Learns instantaneous functions of the input whose outputs vary as slowly as possible, minimizing ⟨ẏ²⟩ under zero-mean, unit-variance and decorrelation constraints, solved in closed form within a fixed (usually quadratic) expansion by sphering and taking the smallest eigenvectors of the derivative covariance. Stacked modules in a 1-D model of the visual hierarchy learn translation, size, rotation, contrast and, less well, illumination invariance from the training stimulus, with location ("where") among the slowest outputs alongside identity ("what"). | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-971](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-971.md)) in full, from Wiskott's own PostScript preprint; worth reading for the slowness objective stated exactly (minimize ⟨ẏ²⟩ under zero mean, unit variance and decorrelation), for its closed-form solution within a fixed nonlinear expansion by sphering and an eigendecomposition of the derivative covariance ([THEORY-746](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-746.md)), and for the demonstration that stacked modules learn translation, size, rotation, contrast and, less well, illumination invariance for 1-D patterns from the training stimulus alone. Read it knowing that optimality holds per module, on the training signal and within the chosen function space, and not for the greedy hierarchy; that "slower is more abstract" is its premise, not a finding, so a stack built this way is slower at higher stages by construction; that the slowest outputs include location, so slowness is not invariance; that no generative model and no learning dynamics appear; and that every stimulus is synthetic and one-dimensional. |
| [LIT-1250](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1250.md) v2 | Diffusion maps, spectral clustering and reaction coordinates of dynamical systems | Nadler, Lafon, Coifman & Kevrekidis (2005; ACHA 2006). For data sampled from p = e^{−U}, it expands the α-normalized diffusion-map operators for small kernel width. The normalized graph Laplacian (α = 0) tends to a backward Fokker–Planck generator with potential 2U, equivalently a Schrödinger operator with potential \|∇U\|² − ΔU. The normalization α = 1/2 gives the generator of the Langevin dynamics ẋ = −∇U + √2ẇ itself. α = 1 gives the Laplace–Beltrami operator, free of the density. So for data from a stochastic system in equilibrium, the leading eigenfunctions approximate the system's slowest modes, and the paper proposes them as reaction coordinates. Examples: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes, where the first eigenfunctions parametrize the slow variable; a double well, where the first eigenfunction is ±1 on the two wells; three wells; and the iris data. The expansions are formal, and the printed generators are twice what the stated kernel and time step give. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-986](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-986.md)) in full, from arXiv:math/0503445v1; worth reading for the bridge from a diffusion map to the dynamics behind the data. For samples from p = e^{−U}, the ordinary normalized graph Laplacian (α = 0) tends to a backward Fokker–Planck generator with potential 2U, and the anisotropic normalization α = 1/2 to the generator of the Langevin dynamics with potential U itself, whose slow eigenfunctions the paper proposes as reaction coordinates. It also has worked examples: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (the finite-ε spectrum λ_k = (τ/(τ+ε))^k), a double well whose first eigenfunction is ±1 on the two wells, and a three-well potential with two pathways. Read it knowing that the generators as printed are twice what the paper's own kernel and time step give (its Ornstein–Uhlenbeck lemma and its equation (32) disagree by that factor, which this reading checked); that "converge" means a formal small-ε expansion of the operator, with the large-sample limit cited and no spectral convergence shown; that its sufficient condition for the first eigenfunctions to depend only on the slow variable is printed the wrong way round; that its double-well example is separable, so the slow coordinate is closed by construction; and that from equilibrium samples the eigenfunctions are recovered well while the slow eigenvalue, the inter-well rate, is not. In what sense slow eigenfunctions are closed coarse variables is the record's addition ([THEORY-762](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-762.md)). The published ACHA version was not reached. |
| [LIT-1256](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1256.md) v3 | Diffusion wavelets | Coifman & Maggioni (2006). A self-adjoint diffusion operator T defines a multiresolution analysis by thresholding its dyadic powers at a precision ε: V_j is spanned by the eigenvectors with λ^t ≥ ε, so the levels are exactly nested spectral bands set by the operator, not by a partition. The contribution is an algorithm that squares T on each compressed orthonormal basis to build localized scaling functions and wavelets for approximations of these spaces, and compressed dyadic powers that apply the Green's function fast. Proofs cover the uncompressed construction; the compressed scheme's error and cost are argued, not proved. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-984](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-984.md)) in full; worth reading for [QUESTION-217](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-217.md) and [QUESTION-218](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-218.md) as the multilevel case of an operator-induced coarse-to-fine hierarchy. The levels V_j are spanned by the eigenvectors of a self-adjoint diffusion T with λ^t ≥ ε at dyadic t. They are exactly nested, the wavelet spaces W_j are spectral bands of about one octave, and a localized orthonormal basis of each level is built without computing eigenvectors. Read it knowing that the levels are spectral bands and not spatial blocks (the dyadic cubes only shape the basis); that nesting needs no spectral decay, which buys only compression; that the compressed algorithm as written thresholds T^{2^{j−1}}, not T^{2^j−1} as §5.4 and Fig. 1 say, and the paper's own Fig. 9 follows the former ([THEORY-758](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-758.md)); that the indexing of V_j is inconsistent between (4.8), §4.6 and Theorem 27; that only the uncompressed route (Theorems 27 and 29) has proofs, while the compressed scheme's error, localization and O(n log² n) cost are argued or observed; and that the non-self-adjoint extension is asserted, not carried out. |
| [LIT-1258](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1258.md) v2 | Exact and Soft Successive Refinement of the Information Bottleneck | Charvin, Catenacci Volpi & Polani (Entropy 2023). Defines successive refinement for the information bottleneck in single-letter form: a coarse optimum T₁ can be extended to a fine optimum (T₁, S). This holds iff some pair of optima forms the chain X → T₂ → T₁, iff the coarse encoder is a garbling of the fine one, and, when the fine decoder is injective, iff the coarse decoder points lie in the convex hull of the fine ones. That last form gives a linear-programming test. Refinability is proved for binary X and Y, for Y a function of X, and (from a cited semigroup result) for jointly Gaussian variables. Numerically, for 3×3 and larger random sources, the hull test on computed optima often fails, especially below the second bifurcation. The loss, measured by unique information, stayed under 5.4% of I(X; T₁, T₂). The failures are not certified, since global optimality and uniqueness of the optima are left as a conjecture. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-981](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-981.md)) in full, from the published version in the University of Hertfordshire Research Archive; worth reading for the single-letter definition of successive refinement for the information bottleneck and its equivalent forms (Proposition 1: some pair of optimal encoders forms the Markov chain X → T₂ → T₁; Proposition 8: the coarse encoder is a Blackwell garbling of the fine one); for the convex-hull test (Proposition 4: with an injective fine decoder, refinement holds iff every decoder point q(X\|t₁) lies in the convex hull of the q(X\|t₂)), checkable by a linear programme; for proofs of refinability when X and Y are both binary, when Y is a function of X, and for jointly Gaussian variables (the last resting on Kline and Palmer's semigroup result); and for soft refinement measured by unique information. Read it knowing that the linear programme tests the particular optima a solver returns, so that a failed test certifies nothing unless the optima are globally optimal and unique, which the paper leaves as Conjecture 1 and calls its own figures "mere numerical proxies" (Appendix D); that its evidence that refinement fails is therefore numerical and uncertified, with no count of how many sampled distributions failed; that the unique information computed is an upper bound on the soft measure for the same reason; that the deep-learning reading of §4.2 is speculative; and that the commentary on Proposition 8 swaps its points (ii) and (iii). |
| [LIT-1261](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1261.md) v2 | On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks | Rahaman et al. (2019; arXiv 2018). Proves, for compactly supported ReLU networks, that the Fourier transform falls as k^(−d−1) in almost every direction and no slower than k^(−2). Shows by experiment that a deep ReLU network fits low frequencies before high ones, even when the high ones are ten times stronger, and that its high-frequency components are the least robust to parameter noise. Shows that on a curve embedded in the plane, high latent frequencies are fitted more easily as the embedding gets longer and more convoluted. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-983](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-983.md)) in full; worth reading for the experiment in which a ReLU network fits low frequencies before high ones even when the high ones are ten times stronger ([THEORY-759](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-759.md)), for the Fourier analysis of piecewise-linear networks ([THEORY-761](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-761.md)), and for the observation that the frequencies that are hard to learn depend on how the data's manifold is embedded. Read it knowing that its theorem is proved only for compactly supported networks, that the link from the theorem to the order of learning is an upper bound on speed and not a proof of order, that the volume result in Appendix D does not follow, and that its "manifold complexity" is confounded with the curve's length. |

| [LIT-1293](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1293.md) | Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 3: Generative AI Training (Pre-Publication Version) | U.S. Copyright Office (2025), pre-publication version. Collecting, curating and training on copyrighted works implicate the reproduction right; model weights do so only where they have memorized substantially similar expression. Whether the copying is excused is a fair-use question, use by use. Training a foundation model will often be transformative, but less so the more its outputs serve the originals' purpose; the non-expressive and human-learning arguments are rejected; market dilution is cognizable harm. The Office recommends letting licensing markets develop, with extended collective licensing if they fail. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1024](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1024.md)) in full, in the pre-publication version of 9 May 2025, the only version copyright.gov offers on that date; worth reading as the official US statement of where training touches copyright (collection, curation, training copies, and model weights only where they have memorized a work), as an application of the Warhol v. Goldsmith use-specific test of transformative purpose to generative training (a spectrum, from research and closed non-substitutive deployments to fine-tuning that reproduces a series's characters), and for its new market-dilution theory of harm under the fourth factor. Read it knowing that it is an agency's analysis, not a holding; that it predates the 2025 district-court rulings on training; that its account of the facts rests mostly on the parties' own comments; that the dilution theory is offered as "uncharted territory" with no data; and that a final version was promised but had not appeared by 2026-10-20. |
| [LIT-1296](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1296.md) v2 | Slow Feature Analysis as Variational Inference Objective | Schüler & Wiskott (arXiv 2025). With a Gaussian random-walk prior on the latents, an instantaneous unit-variance Gaussian encoder N(g(x_t), I) and an arbitrary forward model, the evidence lower bound is a sum of per-point reconstruction terms minus ½Σ‖g(x_{t−1}) − g(x_t)‖², the unordered slowness loss. The reconstruction term then does the work of SFA's unit-variance and decorrelation constraints, by argument, not proof. The authors say this "does not lead to full equivalence" with SFA. For linear Gaussian encoder and decoder they give the objective and the necessary condition VᵀV = WᵀĊW, and no optimum. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1015](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1015.md)) in full, from arXiv v1; worth reading for an exact identity, not a limit: with a Markov prior p(z_t \| z_{t−1}) = N(z_{t−1}, I) (a Gaussian random walk, no decay), an instantaneous encoder q(z_t \| x_t) = N(g(x_t), I) and any forward model p_θ(x_t \| z_t), the KL half of the ELBO is the unordered slowness loss ½Σ‖g(x_{t−1}) − g(x_t)‖² (plus a constant the paper drops), so the ELBO is a per-point reconstruction term minus a slowness term (Eq. 40), and the reconstruction term takes the place of SFA's unit-variance and decorrelation constraints; and for the linear Gaussian case (Eq. 41) and its necessary condition VᵀV = WᵀĊW (Eq. 42). Read it knowing that the paper does not claim, and does not have, equivalence to SFA: it derives no optimum, so what its objective learns is the record's derivation in [THEORY-775](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-775.md) (on whitened input, the span of the slowest SFA directions whose lag-one autocorrelation exceeds ½, rotation unidentified; on raw input, not SFA's subspace and not scale-invariant); that the constant d/2 per step is cancelled by an error in Eq. 35; that Eq. 41 has the sign of the reconstruction error reversed (the appendix's Eq. 54 is right); that Eq. 42 is necessary, not "equivalent" to stationarity as §7 says; that the prior builds in independent, non-decaying latents, so closure of the latent coordinates is assumed, not found; and that its account of Turner and Sahani (2007) is two sentences of related work, which the record has not checked against that paper ([LIT-1287](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1287.md), Unavailable). |
| [LIT-1309](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1309.md) v2 | A Theory of Usable Information Under Computational Constraints | Xu, Zhao, Song, Stewart & Ermon (2020). Predictive V-information, H_V(Y) − H_V(Y \| X) with the conditional entropies taken as the least expected log loss over a predictive family V, is the information about Y that a predictor restricted to V can use. It recovers Shannon mutual information when V is unrestricted and the coefficient of determination for linear-Gaussian V, is non-negative and zero under independence, can be asymmetric, can be raised by computing on X, and can be estimated with PAC guarantees from the Rademacher complexity of V. | Active — read 2026-10-21 ([NOTE-1048](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1048.md)) in full, from arXiv:2002.10689v1, the ICLR 2020 camera-ready; worth reading as the usable-information literature the record lacked: it defines predictive V-information, the information a predictor restricted to a family V can extract, shows that computation can create it (so the data-processing inequality fails for it), and bounds its estimation error by the Rademacher complexity of V ([THEORY-846](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-846.md), [THEORY-840](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-840.md)). Read it knowing that the failure of the data-processing inequality is shown by informal examples (decryption, feature learning), not by a theorem, that V-information is not bounded by Shannon information unless V's input-free predictions include the true marginal (the record's counterexample, [THEORY-846](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-846.md)), that Proposition 1.2's "mean absolute deviation" is the deviation about the geometric median, and that the experiments are small. |
| [LIT-1326](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1326.md) v2 | Algorithmic monoculture and social welfare | Kleinberg & Raghavan (2021). In a model of two firms hiring from one pool by noisy rankings, if both use the same algorithm, even one more accurate than their private rankings, the quality of decisions can fall without any shocks: under two conditions on the ranking model, for every private accuracy there is a more accurate shared algorithm that is strictly dominant for both firms and lowers both firms' utility and social welfare, a Braess paradox. The Mallows model always meets the conditions; Plackett–Luce never does. | Active — read 2026-10-21 ([NOTE-1033](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1033.md)), from arXiv:2101.05853v2: the main text and Appendices A, B and E in full, Appendices C, D and F in statement; worth reading for the exact conditions under which a shared, more accurate screening algorithm is dominant for every firm and still lowers welfare without any shock ([THEORY-835](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-835.md)), and for the identity that makes independence valuable to a second mover. Read it knowing that the model has two firms hiring one candidate each, that the conditions hold for Mallows rankings always, for Gaussian and Laplacian random utility models with three candidates, and never for Plackett–Luce, and that the losses measured are small (about 4% in one instance). |
| [LIT-1336](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1336.md) v2 | Performative Prediction | Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner & Hardt (2020). When a deployed prediction changes the distribution of the outcomes it predicts, define performative stability (a model optimal for the distribution it induces) and performative optimality (least risk on the distribution it induces); show they can differ; prove that with a smooth, strongly convex loss and a distribution map ε-Lipschitz in Wasserstein distance, retraining converges to a unique stable point when ε < γ/β, that each condition is needed, and that stable points lie within 2L_zε/γ of optima. | Active — read 2026-10-21 ([NOTE-1044](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1044.md)) in full, from arXiv:2002.06673v4; worth reading for the split between performative stability (optimal for the distribution one's own deployment induces, the fixed point of retraining) and performative optimality, for the exact conditions under which retraining converges to a unique stable point (smooth, strongly convex loss and ε < γ/β, each shown necessary; [THEORY-861](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-861.md)), and for the bound 2L_zε/γ between stable points and optima ([THEORY-839](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-839.md)). Read it knowing that its conditions hold in its own simulation only at the smallest ε, that the distribution map depends on the current model alone, and that it says nothing about how to reach the optimum. |
